Vertex Inc · Senior Principal Engineer, AIaaS Enablement (Commercial AI Center of Excellence) · interview cards

Vertex AIaaS Interview Cards

The role asks for three people in one: the technical authority who sets the standards every AI system in the Commercial AI Center of Excellence is built to, an engineer who still trains, fine-tunes and evaluates models by hand, and a leader who grows Principal and Staff engineers. The fourteen cards take the job description line by line: what the line means in practice, what you have done that answers it, how you would do it on Azure, where it goes wrong, the code, and the one-minute answer. Three reference cards close it: the script, the job description mapped against your evidence, and the probes to expect.

Click a card. Every topic card has six tabs: Concepts (with a figure), Evidence, Method on Azure, Pitfalls, Code, and Say it in the room. Chips say where a claim comes from: resume is the resume you sent Vertex, your account is what you have said about the work and recorded in the AIaaS article of 17 October, illustrative marks numbers and designs made up for an example, and dated source tags mark public documents. Azure names are as documented in October 2026 (Microsoft Foundry, Foundry Agent Service, Azure API Management’s AI gateway); preview features are labelled. The worked examples use Vertex’s own public products (Smart Categorization, Vertex Copilot, the Configuration Agent for Dynamics 365) as settings, never as claims about how Vertex builds them. Scenario round? Start with How to run a scenario, then K (the requirements question sheet) and J (the rules: which pattern, which plane, which tool), and the scenario cards A to I and L: each takes a Vertex situation through Architecture logic, Agentic logic, Engineering logic and Evaluation, with the follow-ups and the one-minute answer. 1 · Technical vision, reference architecture and paved roads

A vision for internal AI-as-a-Service is a short list of things that will be true for every product team in three years, a reference architecture that shows where each of them lives, and standards that are cheaper to follow than to avoid. The test of all three is adoption: a standard that no team’s code calls is a wiki page.

From the job descriptionSet the multi-year technical vision, reference architectures, and enterprise standards for AIaaS across PDD, and act as the final technical authority and escalation point for the organization’s hardest AI problems.
the non-negotiable
every production model call goes through one gateway, because identity, quotas, safety, metering and tracing all depend on it
the three contracts
model aliases · retrieve with trimming before ranking · an agent runtime that guarantees identity, budgets, tracing, memory, governed tools and approvals
the measure
share of traffic on the gateway, time to a team’s first call, cost per outcome, and the escape-hatch rate
the authority
decide rarely, in writing, against criteria published in advance; everything routine is self-service

Definitions

Paved road

The supported way to build: templates, SDK, pipeline and defaults that already satisfy the standards. Teams may leave it; it should never be faster to.

Reference architecture

The layers, their contracts and the services that implement them on this cloud, with the decisions that made them, so a team can build without asking.

Standard versus guideline

A standard is enforced by something that runs (policy, gateway, CI). A guideline is advice. Keep the first list short and the second honest.

Final technical authority

The person who closes one-way-door decisions and escalations, in writing, when the criteria do not settle them. Used rarely, or it becomes the bottleneck.

Staying hands-on

Own one critical component in code (the gateway policy fragment or the evaluation harness), read every high-tier design before it ships, and take the hardest incident of the month yourself. That is what keeps the standards honest: you feel their cost first.

BadThe vision is a slide of product logos.
GoodThe vision is a list of statements that will be true for every team, each with a date and a metric.
BadStandards enforced by a review board that meets weekly.

GoodOne mandate, gateway traffic, spent after the road is already faster; everything else wins on speed.

Standards as code: one inventory, three consumers

The inventory is the control plane’s source of truth. The gateway’s alias list, the Azure Policy assignments and the CI gate are generated from it, so a standard cannot drift between the three. illustrative values

# platform/inventory.yaml
aliases:
  chat-default:     {pool: chat-default-pool, family: gpt-4.1,      residency: us, tiers: [low, medium, high]}
  chat-small:       {pool: chat-small-pool,   family: gpt-4.1-mini, residency: us, tiers: [low, medium, high]}
  chat-eu-resident: {pool: chat-eu-pool,      family: gpt-4.1,      residency: eu, tiers: [medium, high]}
  embed-v2:         {pool: embed-v2-pool,     family: text-embedding-3-large, tiers: [low, medium, high]}

workloads:
  product-categorization:
    owner: team-categorization
    tier: high                         # decides the controls: approvals, allowed aliases, evidence pack
    aliases: [chat-default, chat-small, embed-v2]
    golden_set: golden/categorization-v12.jsonl
    gates: {category_accuracy: 0.95, abstain_precision: 0.98}
    data: {training_allowed: false, retention_days: 30}   # card 5: no training without a rights basis
# ci/check_inventory.py: fails the platform pipeline when a workload breaks a standard
import sys, yaml

inv = yaml.safe_load(open("platform/inventory.yaml"))
errors = []
for name, w in inv["workloads"].items():
    if not w.get("golden_set"):
        errors.append(f"{name}: no golden set")
    for alias in w["aliases"]:
        spec = inv["aliases"].get(alias)
        if spec is None:
            errors.append(f"{name}: unknown alias {alias}")
        elif w["tier"] not in spec.get("tiers", []):
            errors.append(f"{name}: alias {alias} not allowed at tier {w['tier']}")
    if w["tier"] == "high" and not w.get("gates"):
        errors.append(f"{name}: high tier needs blocking gates")
if errors:
    sys.exit("\n".join(errors))

In the room

What is your technical vision for AIaaS here?I would build it as a product with one non-negotiable and three contracts. The non-negotiable is that every production model call goes through one gateway, because identity, quotas, safety, metering and tracing all depend on it. The contracts are model aliases, a retrieve service that trims by entitlement before ranking, and an agent runtime that guarantees identity, budgets, tracing, governed tools and approvals. Year one is that road plus two lighthouse workloads; year two is shared capabilities on it, a tool registry, a model factory, evaluation as a service; year three is governed autonomy, agents with their own identities and human approvals. I measure myself on adoption: how much traffic is on the road and how fast a new team gets its first call.
How do you act as the final technical authority without becoming a bottleneck?By publishing the criteria so most decisions never reach me. Routine work is self-service; reversible cross-team decisions go to a rotating design review with a two-day answer; I close the one-way doors, vendor commitments, reservations, the data-rights policy, in a written record with the options, the dissent and a date to revisit. If people wait on me, the criteria are wrong, and I fix them.
How do you stay hands-on at this level?I own one critical component in code, today that would be the gateway policy or the evaluation harness, I read every high-tier design before it ships, and I take the hardest incident of the month myself. At Capital Group I build the agent workflows and the evaluation gates on the platform I designed; that is how I know what my standards cost a team.
Tell me about a reference architecture you established.Capital Group’s Marketing Process Automation, for a $3.2 trillion asset manager. Kong in front of every model call; a supervisor and specialist sub-agents in one Bedrock AgentCore runtime, chosen for shared state, fewer hops and cost, with the split over a gateway and MCP documented as the upgrade path; retrieval as a tool over pgvector and a retrieval-only Neptune graph of the compliance rules; Langfuse with cost per step; Terraform and GitHub Actions; evaluation as a gate before any prompt or model is promoted; human review as a first-class step. On Azure that is API Management, Foundry, AI Search and Agent Service, with the same contracts.

2 · Build, buy or wrap; choosing models and vendors; the long bets

Buy what is undifferentiated and maturing fast, build what encodes your domain and your data, and put a thin layer of your own contracts between the two so that every purchase stays replaceable. Choose models the way you ship them: on your own evaluation set, at your own traffic mix, with cost per correct outcome as the deciding number once the quality gate is passed.

From the job descriptionDrive build-versus-buy, model and vendor selection, and long-term architectural bets, anticipating where the field is heading and preparing the organization to adopt it.
the test
would a customer notice if a competitor had the same thing? If not, buy it or wrap it
the wrap
aliases, retrieve, runtime guarantees and OpenTelemetry keep any vendor a routing change
model choice
quality gate on your golden set first, then cost per correct outcome, latency, residency and contract terms
the bets
open tool and agent protocols, evaluation sets as the durable asset, small specialised models, durable agents

Two questions place every component: does it differentiate, and is the market mature?

Choosing a model on Azure, as a repeatable procedure

  1. Write the decision record first. Problem, options (build, buy, wrap, wait), criteria with weights, exit cost, decision, the date to revisit.
  2. Shortlist from the Foundry catalogue by residency, modality and deployment type, then deploy each candidate as a temporary alias in the test pool (cand-a, cand-b).
  3. Run the workload’s golden set through the gateway with the production prompt, so token counts, latency and safety filtering are what production will see.
  4. Gate, then rank. Drop anything that fails compliance or the quality gate; rank the rest on cost per correct outcome and p95 latency.
  5. Ship by remapping the alias (pool membership), keep the previous model in the pool at weight zero for rollback, and watch online evaluation for a week.
  6. Re-run quarterly, and whenever a new model family lands in the catalogue.

Worked example: product-to-tax-category mapping illustrative numbers

A setting like Vertex’s Smart Categorization, which proposes a tax category per product with a confidence score for a person to approve Vertex data sheet, Apr 2026. Gate: accuracy ≥ 0.95 on 2,000 held-out products. Prices are placeholders: $2.50 / $10 per million input / output tokens for the frontier alias, $0.40 / $1.60 for the small one; 900 input and 60 output tokens per product.

CandidateAccuracyCost per 1,000 productsp95 latencyCost per 1,000 correctGate
frontier model (chat-default)0.94$2.853.1 s$3.03fail
small model (chat-small)0.89$0.461.4 s$0.51fail
fine-tuned small model0.93$0.100.4 s$0.11fail
cascade: fine-tuned model, frontier below 0.8 confidence (15%)0.96$0.533.5 s$0.55pass

The winner is an architecture, not a model: the fine-tuned model is right 98% of the time on the 85% of products it is confident about, and the frontier model takes the hard 15%. Accuracy 0.85 × 0.98 + 0.15 × 0.85 ≈ 0.96; cost $0.10 + 0.15 × $2.85 ≈ $0.53 per 1,000. Card 12 takes the same numbers to a million products a month.

How these decisions go wrong

BadChoosing a model from a public leaderboard.
GoodChoosing on your golden set, through your gateway, at your traffic mix.
BadPrice per million tokens as the metric.
GoodCost per correct outcome, after the quality gate; a cheap wrong answer is the most expensive kind.
BadBuying one vendor’s whole architecture: its agents, memory, evaluation and tracing, with no contract of your own between them.
GoodBuying the engines and wrapping each behind your contracts, so each can be replaced alone.
BadBuilding commodity: your own gateway, your own vector database.
GoodBuying the commodity and building the policy, the evaluation and the domain tools on top.
BadNo exit plan until the price rises.
GoodExit cost written into the decision record on day one.
BadA decision made once and never revisited.
GoodA quarterly re-run of the scorecard; the alias makes the switch cheap.

The scorecard as code: candidates through the gateway on the golden set

import json, time, statistics
from openai import AzureOpenAI
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential, get_bearer_token_provider

PRICE = {"chat-default": (2.50, 10.00), "chat-small": (0.40, 1.60), "cand-ft": (0.20, 0.80)}  # $ per 1M in/out: placeholders
client = AzureOpenAI(
    azure_endpoint="https://gw.example.com/ai",          # the gateway, so tokens and filters match production
    api_version="2024-10-21",
    azure_ad_token_provider=get_bearer_token_provider(DefaultAzureCredential(), "api://ai-platform-gateway/.default"),
)

def score(alias: str, rows: list[dict]) -> dict:
    correct, cost, lat = 0, 0.0, []
    for r in rows:                                     # r = {"messages": [...], "label": "..."}
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(model=alias, messages=r["messages"], temperature=0,
                                              response_format={"type": "json_object"})
        lat.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
        pred = json.loads(resp.choices[0].message.content).get("category")
        correct += int(pred == r["label"])
        p_in, p_out = PRICE[alias]
        cost += (resp.usage.prompt_tokens * p_in + resp.usage.completion_tokens * p_out) / 1e6
    return {"alias": alias, "accuracy": round(correct / len(rows), 3),
            "cost_per_1k": round(1000 * cost / len(rows), 2),
            "p95_s": round(statistics.quantiles(lat, n=20)[18], 2),
            "cost_per_1k_correct": round(1000 * cost / max(correct, 1), 2)}

rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("golden/categorization-v12.jsonl")]
board = sorted((score(a, rows) for a in PRICE), key=lambda s: s["cost_per_1k_correct"])
passing = [s for s in board if s["accuracy"] >= 0.95]      # gate first, then rank
print(json.dumps(passing or board, indent=2))
<!-- decisions/ADR-014-categorization-model.md : the record that closes a one-way door -->
# ADR-014 Model for product-to-category mapping
Status: accepted · Decider: Senior Principal, CAI CoE · Revisit: 2027-01-15
Context: 1M products/month, accuracy gate 0.95, US residency, approval by a tax analyst below 0.8 confidence
Options: frontier alias · small alias · fine-tuned small model · cascade (fine-tuned, frontier on low confidence)
Criteria: gate (compliance, accuracy) → cost per correct outcome → p95 latency → exit cost
Decision: cascade. Evidence: eval run 2026-10-19 on golden v12 (link). Exit: alias remap, adapters retrained in 2 days
Dissent: catalog team prefers frontier-only for simplicity; revisit if escalation rate exceeds 25%

In the room

How do you decide build versus buy?Two questions: does it differentiate Vertex, and is the market mature? Commodity that is maturing, the gateway, content safety, embeddings, I buy. Anything that encodes our tax knowledge or our customers’ data, the golden sets, the evaluators, the MCP servers over the tax engine, the categorization models, I build. Most of the platform is the third answer: buy the engine and own the contract, so AI Search sits behind our retrieve and Agent Service behind our runtime rules. Every decision record names the exit cost before we sign.
How do you choose between models and vendors?On our golden set, through our gateway, at our traffic mix. Compliance and the quality gate are pass or fail; then cost per correct outcome, latency, operability and exit cost. Often the winner is an architecture: a fine-tuned small model for the confident majority and a frontier model for the hard tail beats either alone on accuracy and cost. Shipping is an alias remap, and the old model stays in the pool for rollback.
Where is the field heading, and what would you bet on?Open protocols for tools and agents, so I would register every tool as an MCP server behind the gateway now. Evaluation sets as the asset that outlives every model. Small specialised models for volume tasks. And durable agents that run for days with human approvals. Each bet has a cheap preparation today and a signal that tells us when to double down.
Tell me about a build-versus-buy decision you made.At Xiom.AI we used existing tools for the data, Helium10, Jungle Scout, Google Analytics and Linnworks, and built the decision layer on top; that layer produced $1.5M in saved and added revenue and 89% forecast accuracy. Earlier, at innogy’s innovation hub, evaluating startups’ AI was my job, which is where I learned to ask for the exit cost first.

3 · The model-training strategy, from classic ML to LLMs

A training strategy is three things: a rule for which problems get which kind of model, a factory that turns approved data into evaluated and versioned models, and the discipline to climb the ladder only when the rung below has been measured and found short. Most enterprise prediction problems still belong to classic ML; the job is knowing which ones do not.

From the job descriptionDefine and own the enterprise model-training strategy across traditional AI/ML and LLMs, and personally train, fine-tune (e.g., QLoRA, LoRA, PEFT, and full fine-tuning), and evaluate models when the problem demands it.
the ladder
prompt → retrieval → tools → fine-tune → distil → domain pre-training; climb only with evidence
classic ML keeps
tabular prediction, forecasting, ranking at low latency, anomaly detection: cheaper, faster, explainable
LLMs take
language-shaped inputs, long-tail categories, extraction, reasoning over documents, tool use
the factory
dataset card → training job → evaluation gate → registry → alias; one path for a gradient-boosted model and a LoRA adapter

The adaptation ladder, with a classic-ML lane beside it

Which problem gets which model illustrative examples in a tax-software setting

Problem shapeDefaultWhyExample
Tabular predictionGradient boosting (LightGBM, XGBoost)Fast, cheap, strong on tabular data, explainable with SHAPWhich customer implementations will slip
Time seriesA forecaster with exogenous drivers (NeuralProphet, boosted lags)Seasonality, holidays, filing calendarsSupport-case or transaction-volume forecast
Text classification with a long tail of labelsFine-tuned small model, frontier model for low confidenceLanguage-shaped input; thousands of categoriesProduct description → tax category
Extraction from documentsModel with a JSON schema; fine-tune if the format keeps driftingVariable layouts, fixed output contractFields from an exemption certificate or an invoice
Questions over contentRetrieval plus a frontier model, with citationsKnowledge changes daily; answers must citeProduct-documentation and tax-content Q&A
Actions in business systemsAn agent with tools around a deterministic engineThe engine computes the tax; the model plans and explainsA tax-configuration change proposed in an ERP
Ranking and suggestionsTwo-tower retrieval plus a rankerLatency at scale; learns from clicksSuggesting categories or rules to an analyst

What the strategy commits every team to

  • A baseline before a model. The cheapest rung is run on the golden set first; its score is the number every later rung must beat.
  • Error analysis before a climb. Two hundred failures labelled by cause; the dominant cause names the next rung.
  • One factory. The same data registration, evaluation gate, registry and alias promotion for classic and generative models.
  • An owner, a tier and a retirement rule for every model. A model whose task a cheaper rung now solves is retired, not kept warm.

Fifteen years of classic ML, and the deep models on top

  • Allianz. “Churn, next-best-product, risk, propensity, customer-lifetime-value and personalization models with actuaries and digital stakeholders, improving accuracy by 20% versus baselines”; the Automatic Predictive Modeler with SVMs and gradient boosting. resume
  • Xiom.AI. Forecasting and pricing with XGBoost and NeuralProphet: “89% forecast accuracy”, “15% better stock handling”. resume
  • E.ON. Optiheat district-heating optimisation with time-series forecasting, NeuralProphet, autoencoders and MLOps pipelines on Azure Data Factory, Databricks and Azure ML, “cutting cloud cost by 25%”; anomaly detection, geospatial scoring and drone-image computer vision with CNNs, VAEs and semantic segmentation. resume
  • E.ON customer service. “Customer-service GenAI/chatbot capabilities (Hugging Face Transformers, LSTM with self-attention, Flask, CI/CD), improving intent accuracy by 30%.” resume
  • Virtual Minds. “Trained and deployed a two-tower deep neural ranking model at 10K QPS” with daily incremental updates; price-elasticity and demand-forecasting models for bid floors. resume
  • Noctal. “Shipped multimodal models (ViT, Audio Spectrogram Transformers, Stable Diffusion) on GCP Vertex AI, GKE and GPU/TPU serving — 80% throughput uplift, 90% user-engagement lift.” resume

Why this landsFew candidates for an LLM-heavy role can say “gradient boosting first” with fifteen years of production evidence and also ship deep and generative models. The strategy card is where that breadth is the answer, not a footnote.
Say it before they doYou have owned the training approach for a team and a portfolio (E.ON’s fifteen people, Noctal’s research and MLE groups), not yet as the enterprise standard for a whole product organisation. Frame the factory as the E.ON function scaled through a platform.

Running the strategy on Azure

  1. Inventory problems, not models. For each product team: the AI task, volume, latency budget, cost of an error, labelled data available, and the current approach.
  2. Place each on the ladder with evidence. Run the cheapest rung on the golden set; label two hundred failures by cause; climb only to the rung that fixes the dominant cause.
  3. Classic ML on Azure Machine Learning. AutoML for a first baseline, then training jobs in pipelines (LightGBM or XGBoost), MLflow tracking, batch or managed online endpoints.
  4. LLM adaptation on Foundry or Azure ML. Foundry fine-tuning jobs for hosted models (supervised, preference DPO, or reinforcement fine-tuning where the model supports it; Standard, Global or Developer training tiers) Foundry docs, updated Sep 2026. Azure ML GPU jobs for open-weight models with your own PEFT code (card 4).
  5. One registry, one promotion path. Each model is registered with its data version, code commit and evaluation report; it deploys as a new version behind an alias; online evaluation watches it; rollback is an alias change.
  6. Review the portfolio each quarter. Retire models a cheaper rung now matches; re-run the scorecard (card 2) when a new model family lands.

Worked example: error analysis picks the rung illustrative

Product-to-tax-category mapping with a frontier model and a few-shot prompt scores 0.94 against a 0.95 gate. Two hundred failures, labelled by cause:

Cause of the errorShareRung that fixes itChange
Long-tail categories the model rarely chooses41%fine-tuneSFT on approved mappings, oversampling the tail
Description too thin (no material, use or size)27%toolsA catalogue-lookup tool for attributes; abstain when absent
Category definitions changed (new codes, holiday rules)18%retrievalRetrieve the current category definitions by effective date
Wrong label in the golden set14%noneFix the label; re-baseline

Fixing labels first moves the baseline; the fine-tune then targets the largest real cause, and the tool and retrieval fixes go in alongside it because they are cheaper. Card 4 trains the adapter; card 12 prices the result at a million products a month.

How a training strategy fails

BadFine-tuning to add knowledge that changes every month.
GoodRetrieval for knowledge; fine-tuning for behaviour, format, style and the long tail of a stable task.
BadAn LLM for a tabular prediction.
GoodA gradient-boosted baseline first; an LLM only where the input is language-shaped.
BadStarting at the top of the ladder because it is interesting.
GoodStarting at the bottom and climbing on error analysis.
BadA fine-tune judged only on the task it was trained for.
GoodA regression suite for general capability and safety beside the task metric.
BadSeparate pipelines, registries and promotion rules for classic and generative models.
GoodOne factory; the model type is a parameter.
BadModels nobody owns, kept running after their task moved.
GoodAn owner, a tier, a monitoring plan and a retirement rule for every model in the inventory.

The two ends of the factory: a classic baseline and a hosted fine-tune

# 1. Classic ML on Azure ML: a LightGBM baseline as a pipeline step, tracked with MLflow
from azure.ai.ml import MLClient, command, Input
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

ml = MLClient(DefaultAzureCredential(), SUBSCRIPTION, RESOURCE_GROUP, WORKSPACE)
job = command(
    code="./train",
    command="python train.py --data ${{inputs.data}} --target slipped",
    inputs={"data": Input(type="uri_folder", path="azureml:implementation-features:7")},  # versioned data asset
    environment="azureml:lightgbm-env:3", compute="cpu-cluster",
    experiment_name="implementation-risk", display_name="lgbm-baseline",
)
ml.jobs.create_or_update(job)

# train/train.py
import argparse, mlflow, lightgbm as lgb, pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(); ap.add_argument("--data"); ap.add_argument("--target"); a = ap.parse_args()
df = pd.read_parquet(a.data)
X, y = df.drop(columns=[a.target]), df[a.target]
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=7)
mlflow.lightgbm.autolog()
model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=600, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=31).fit(Xtr, ytr)
mlflow.log_metric("test_auc", roc_auc_score(yte, model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]))
# 2. A hosted fine-tune on Foundry: supervised, LoRA under the hood, chat-format JSONL
from openai import AzureOpenAI
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential, get_bearer_token_provider

client = AzureOpenAI(azure_endpoint=FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT, api_version="2025-04-01-preview",
                     azure_ad_token_provider=get_bearer_token_provider(
                         DefaultAzureCredential(), "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default"))
train = client.files.create(file=open("data/taxcat-train-v3.jsonl", "rb"), purpose="fine-tune")
valid = client.files.create(file=open("data/taxcat-valid-v3.jsonl", "rb"), purpose="fine-tune")
job = client.fine_tuning.jobs.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14",
    training_file=train.id, validation_file=valid.id, suffix="taxcat-v3", seed=7,
    method={"type": "supervised",
            "supervised": {"hyperparameters": {"n_epochs": 2, "learning_rate_multiplier": 0.1}}},
)
print(job.id, job.status)   # the training tier (Standard, Global, Developer) is chosen per job; check the docs for the field

Each training row is one chat in JSONL, e.g. {"messages": [{"role": "system", ...}, {"role": "user", "content": "Organic cotton baby onesie, 3–6 months"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "{\"category\": \"...\"}"}]}. Foundry needs at least 10 rows and suggests starting near 50; real gains need hundreds to thousands, and the system message at inference must match training Foundry docs, updated Sep 2026.

In the room

What is your model-training strategy?A ladder, a portfolio rule and a factory. The ladder is prompt, retrieval, tools, fine-tuning, distillation, and only very rarely pre-training; a team climbs a rung when error analysis on its golden set says the next rung fixes the dominant error. The portfolio rule is that tabular prediction, forecasting and ranking default to classic ML, and language-shaped problems go to LLMs. The factory is one path for both: registered data, a training job, an evaluation gate, the registry, then an alias. And every model has an owner and a retirement rule.
When do you fine-tune instead of prompting or retrieval?Retrieval when the model lacks facts, because facts change and fine-tuning bakes them in. Tools when it needs an exact answer, like a tax calculation the engine already computes. Fine-tuning when the task is stable and the errors are behavioural: a long tail of categories, a format that drifts, a house style; and I need hundreds to thousands of approved examples. Distillation when volume makes cost the problem.
Where does traditional ML still win?Anywhere the data is a table. At Allianz our churn, risk and lifetime-value models beat the baselines by 20%; at Xiom.AI gradient boosting and NeuralProphet gave 89% forecast accuracy; at Virtual Minds a two-tower model served 10K queries per second. An LLM would have been slower, costlier and harder to explain in every one of those.
How would you set training standards across many teams?Make the standard the pipeline. A dataset card with a rights basis before data is usable, a baseline before a model, error analysis before a climb, a regression suite beside the task metric, registration with lineage, and promotion only through an alias. Teams get it by using the template, not by reading a document.

4 · Fine-tuning by hand: LoRA, QLoRA, PEFT and full fine-tuning

Fine-tuning changes a model’s behaviour by updating weights on examples of the behaviour you want. Full fine-tuning updates every weight and needs about sixteen bytes of GPU memory per parameter before activations; LoRA freezes the model and trains two thin matrices beside each chosen layer, about half a percent of the parameters; QLoRA does the same over a 4-bit copy of the frozen model, which is why a 7B model trains on one ordinary GPU. The engineering is in the data, the evaluation, and knowing when not to fine-tune at all.

From the job description… and personally train, fine-tune (e.g., QLoRA, LoRA, PEFT, and full fine-tuning), and evaluate models when the problem demands it.
LoRA
h = W·x + (α/r)·B·A·x; B is d×r and starts at zero, A is r×k; only A and B train
QLoRA
frozen base in 4-bit NF4 with double quantisation, adapters in bf16, paged optimiser states
full fine-tuning
≈ 16 bytes per parameter with mixed-precision Adam, before activations; shard it with FSDP or ZeRO-3
objectives
SFT imitates demonstrations, DPO learns from preference pairs, RFT optimises a grader’s reward

What LoRA trains, and what each method costs in memory for a 7B model

The parameter-efficient family

MethodWhat trainsShare of a 7B modelUse it when
LoRALow-rank A and B beside chosen linear layers; merge into W for serving or keep as a swappable adapter0.1–1%The default for SFT and DPO
QLoRALoRA over a frozen base stored in 4-bit NF4 with double quantisation; paged optimiser0.1–1%One GPU, larger bases, cost-sensitive teams; the paper fits 65B on one 48 GB GPU
DoRASplits each weight into magnitude and direction; LoRA on the direction≈ LoRALoRA underfits at a given rank
Prompt / prefix tuningLearned virtual tokens prepended to the input or to each layer< 0.1%Many light tasks on one frozen model
Bottleneck adapters, IA³Small inserted MLPs, or learned scaling vectors0.01–5%Older stacks; tiny budgets
Full fine-tuningEvery weight100%Small models, large domain shifts, or when adapters plateau and the data is large

The objectives

SFT

Cross-entropy on the assistant tokens of demonstrations. Teaches format, style, the long tail of a task. Needs clean, consistent examples more than many.

DPO

Learns from pairs (chosen, rejected) against a frozen reference model, with no reward model: the loss below. Good for analyst corrections and house preferences.

RFT

Reinforcement fine-tuning against graders or verifiable checks; for reasoning tasks with a checkable answer. On Foundry it is offered on reasoning models such as o4-mini.

Distillation

A small student trained on a large teacher’s outputs for one task. The usual path from a frontier prototype to a cheap production model.

DPO: L = −log σ( β · [ log πθ(y_w|x) − log π_ref(y_w|x) − log πθ(y_l|x) + log π_ref(y_l|x) ] )

Starting points that rarely embarrass you tune on validation loss

KnobLoRA / QLoRAFull fine-tuningFoundry hosted job
learning rate1e-4 to 2e-41e-5 to 2e-5learning_rate_multiplier 0.02–0.2
rank, alpha, dropoutr 16 (8–64), α = 2r, 0.05n/aLoRA chosen by the service
target layersall linear layers (the QLoRA paper found this needed to match full fine-tuning)alln/a
epochs1–31–2n_epochs, or automatic
schedulecosine, 3% warm-upcosine, warm-upbatch_size up to 256

Trained models in production for fifteen years; adapters are the newer layer

  • Headline. “Fine-tuning and evaluating models (PyTorch, Hugging Face, LoRA/PEFT).” resume
  • E.ON. Transformer and attention models for customer-service intent, “improving intent accuracy by 30%”. resume
  • Noctal. Multimodal models (ViT, Audio Spectrogram Transformers, Stable Diffusion) shipped on Vertex AI, GKE and GPU/TPU serving, “80% throughput uplift”. resume
  • Virtual Minds. A two-tower deep ranking model trained and deployed “with daily incremental updates, A/B harnesses, statistical gates and rollback paths”: continuous training as an operation. resume
  • Capital Group. “Self-improving agentic workflows” and digital twins of editorial and legal reviewers. resume Turning reviewer decisions into SFT and DPO data is the natural next step to describe as a plan. illustrative
What the panel will testDepth on LLM adaptation specifically. Be ready to draw LoRA and say why B starts at zero, do QLoRA’s memory arithmetic, write the DPO loss, and lay out the evaluation that proves a fine-tune helped. All four are on this card.
Say it before they doMulti-node full fine-tuning of a 30–70B model (FSDP or ZeRO-3 across many GPUs) is not on your resume. Say how you would run it (Code tab), what it costs, and why most enterprise tasks are better served by LoRA on a smaller model plus retrieval.

The fine-tuning recipe on Azure

  1. Baseline. The best prompt with few-shot examples on the frozen model; record the golden-set metric and the regression suite (instruction following, safety evaluators).
  2. Data. Approved examples only, with a rights basis (card 5); split by time or by customer so nothing leaks; de-duplicate near-duplicates across splits; hold out a slice nobody tunes on.
  3. Route. Hosted: Foundry fine-tuning (SFT and DPO on GPT-4.1-family models, RFT on o4-mini, SFT on open models such as Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Qwen-32B, Ministral-3B and gpt-oss-20b; LoRA under the hood) Foundry docs, updated Sep 2026. Self-managed: an Azure ML GPU cluster with PEFT and TRL when you need QLoRA, full fine-tuning, a custom loss or an unsupported base.
  4. Training tier. Standard keeps data and weights in the resource’s region; Global is cheaper and copies them to another region; Developer is cheapest, pre-emptible, with no residency guarantee. Regulated data trains on Standard.
  5. Evaluate. Task metric on the held-out slice, a paired significance test against the baseline, the regression suite, and confidence calibration if the model feeds a cascade.
  6. Ship. Deploy as a new version behind an alias in a pool: shadow, canary, promote; rollback is an alias change. Foundry removes deployments idle for 15 days but keeps the model.
  7. Iterate. When the remaining errors are preferences rather than knowledge, collect analyst corrections as DPO pairs and run a second stage.

Worked example: a small model fine-tuned on approved category mappings illustrative

Metric, 2,000 held-out productsSmall model, few-shotAfter SFT on 12,000 mappings
accuracy0.890.93
recall on tail categories (< 20 training examples)0.610.84
accuracy where confidence ≥ 0.8 (85% of products)0.950.98
expected calibration error0.090.03
prompt tokens per product (no few-shot block)900250
instruction-following regression suitebaseline−0.4 pts (limit −1.0)

Paired test: 31 products the base got right and the tuned model got wrong, 111 the reverse. McNemar χ² = (|31 − 111| − 1)² ÷ 142 ≈ 44, p < 0.001: the gain of 80 ÷ 2,000 = 4 points is not noise. The calibrated confidence is what lets card 2’s cascade send only 15% of products to the frontier model.

How fine-tunes go wrong

BadRandom train and test split over products that share a family or a customer.
GoodSplit by time or by customer and de-duplicate near-duplicates, or the held-out score is a memory test.
BadFine-tuning in facts that change monthly.
GoodRetrieval for facts; fine-tuning for behaviour and the long tail.
BadOnly the task metric reported.
GoodTask metric, paired test, regression suite, safety evaluators and calibration, every time.
BadA full-fine-tuning learning rate on LoRA, or the reverse.
GoodAbout 1e-4 to 2e-4 for adapters, 1e-5 for full weights, watched on validation loss.
BadA different system prompt in production than in training.
GoodThe training system message, versioned with the adapter, used verbatim at inference.
BadRegulated data on a pre-emptible, no-residency training tier to save money.
GoodStandard tier (or your own region’s GPUs) for anything with customer data.
BadMerged weights with no record of the base model or the data.
GoodAdapters versioned with the base model’s hash, the dataset’s content hash and the evaluation report.

QLoRA with PEFT and TRL, full fine-tuning with FSDP, and the paired test

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import LoraConfig, prepare_model_for_kbit_training
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

BASE = "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct"          # any open-weight base you have the rights to adapt
bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
                         bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE, quantization_config=bnb, device_map="auto")
model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model)

lora = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
                  target_modules="all-linear")               # every linear layer, as the QLoRA paper advises
data = load_dataset("json", data_files={"train": "taxcat-train-v3.jsonl", "eval": "taxcat-valid-v3.jsonl"})

args = SFTConfig(output_dir="out/taxcat-qlora", num_train_epochs=2, learning_rate=2e-4,
                 per_device_train_batch_size=8, gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
                 lr_scheduler_type="cosine", warmup_ratio=0.03, bf16=True,
                 gradient_checkpointing=True, optim="paged_adamw_8bit",
                 eval_strategy="steps", eval_steps=200, save_steps=200, logging_steps=20,
                 report_to="mlflow")
trainer = SFTTrainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=data["train"], eval_dataset=data["eval"],
                     peft_config=lora, processing_class=tok)
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("out/taxcat-qlora/adapter")   # the adapter only: tens of MB, versioned with the data hash
# fsdp.yaml: full fine-tuning of an 8B model on one 8-GPU node (16 B/param ≈ 128 GB of state, sharded 8 ways)
distributed_type: FSDP
mixed_precision: bf16
num_processes: 8
fsdp_config:
  fsdp_sharding_strategy: FULL_SHARD
  fsdp_auto_wrap_policy: TRANSFORMER_BASED_WRAP
  fsdp_state_dict_type: SHARDED_STATE_DICT
  fsdp_offload_params: false
# accelerate launch --config_file fsdp.yaml train_full.py --learning_rate 1e-5 --num_train_epochs 1
# did the fine-tune help? a paired test on the same held-out products
from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import mcnemar
both, base_only, tuned_only, neither = 1749, 31, 111, 109        # counts over 2,000 products (illustrative)
res = mcnemar([[both, base_only], [tuned_only, neither]], exact=False, correction=True)
print(round(res.statistic, 1), res.pvalue)                       # ≈ 44.0, p < 0.001

Masking the loss to the assistant tokens matters for chat data; TRL exposes it per dataset type (assistant-only or completion-only loss), and it needs a chat template that marks the assistant turns. Library arguments move between releases; the shapes above are stable.

In the room

Walk me through LoRA.Freeze the pretrained weight W and learn its update as a product of two thin matrices, B times A, with rank r much smaller than the layer, scaled by alpha over r. B starts at zero, so training starts exactly at the base model. At rank 16 on every linear layer of a 7B model that is about 40 million trainable parameters, half a percent. For serving you either merge B·A into W, so there is no latency cost, or keep adapters separate and swap them per task or per tenant on one base model.
Why QLoRA, and what does it cost you?It stores the frozen base in 4-bit NF4, quantises the quantisation constants too, and pages optimiser state, so memory for a 7B model drops from about 14 GB to about 4 GB before activations; the paper fine-tuned 65B on one 48 GB GPU. The cost is slower steps, because weights are de-quantised on the fly, and a small quality risk I check against a bf16 LoRA run on the same data.
When would you do full fine-tuning?When the model is small, the domain shift is large, adapters have plateaued, and I have the data to justify it. It costs about 16 bytes per parameter before activations, so even an 8B model means sharding across a node with FSDP, and it raises the forgetting risk, so the regression suite matters more. For most enterprise tasks LoRA on a smaller model plus retrieval wins on cost and on time to ship.
How do you prove a fine-tune helped?A held-out set split by time or customer, the task metric with a paired test against the baseline, a regression suite for general capability and safety, calibration if confidence drives routing, and then shadow and canary traffic behind an alias. If any of those fails, the adapter does not ship, however good the headline number is.
SFT, DPO or RFT?SFT when I have demonstrations of the right answer. DPO when I have judgements of better and worse, like an analyst correcting a draft; it needs no reward model. RFT when the answer can be checked by a grader, which suits reasoning tasks. In practice SFT first, then DPO on the corrections.

5 · Training data: sourcing, lineage, consent, PII and the pipelines

Training data from commercial AI products is mostly exhaust: what users asked, what a model proposed, what a person approved or corrected. It is the most valuable data the organisation owns and the easiest to misuse. The standard is simple to state: nothing trains a model without a dataset card that says where the data came from, under which right it may be used, what was removed and what its content hash is; and every model can name the dataset versions it learned from, so a deletion request or a licence change can be traced to the models it touches.

From the job descriptionEstablish standards for how and where training data from Commercial AI products is sourced, cleaned, versioned, stored, and governed (lineage, licensing/consent, and PII), and architect the large-scale data and feature pipelines behind them.
sources
approval and correction events, prompts and outputs, documents and tax content, licensed and synthetic data
the right to use
a rights basis per record (contract, consent, licence, owned); customer data trains nothing by default
the record
dataset card + content hash + lineage edges: event → dataset version → training run → model version → alias
PII
detect, then drop, mask or tokenise before the training zone; never rely on a model to forget

From a product event to a model version, with the way back

You have built the pipelines; the governance layer is the standard you add

  • E.ON. Production pipelines on Azure Data Factory, Databricks and Azure ML with MLOps behind Optiheat (“cutting cloud cost by 25%”). resume
  • Telefónica Germany / O2. “Footfall and movement-pattern analytics for retail-location decisions with Scala, Spark, AWS, Kafka streaming and GIS”: large-scale streaming data about people’s movements. resume
  • Allianz. Telematics features (“snap-to-road, accelerometer/gyroscope profiling, Hadoop, Spark, MongoDB”) and “established explainability and monitoring practices” in an insurer. resume
  • Xiom.AI. Four external sources (Helium10, Jungle Scout, Google Analytics, Linnworks) integrated “into a unified AI data model”. resume
  • Virtual Minds and Capital Group. Snowflake, dbt and Airflow in the stack; “knowledge-graph and retrieval integrations for Adobe Workfront, regulatory data and disclosures” with human review of every output. resume
  • Research. A doctorate on spatio-temporal trajectory data: map matching, mobility mining, similarity search. resume
How to frame itYou have run the data side in production on Azure and at streaming scale, in an insurer, a utility, a telco and an asset manager. The rights ledger, dataset cards and lineage-driven deletion are the standard you would add on top, because commercial AI products turn customer interactions into training data, and that needs a contract-level answer before it needs a technical one.
Say it before they doA formal training-data rights ledger is not on your resume. Present it as the design you would put in place, built with Legal and Privacy, and grounded in the regulated settings you know.

The data platform behind the models, on Azure

  1. Zones. OneLake or ADLS Gen2 with three zones: landing (raw, restricted, short retention), curated (rights-filtered and redacted) and training snapshots (immutable). Entra groups per zone, private endpoints, customer-managed keys where contracts ask.
  2. Catalogue and lineage. Microsoft Purview scans and classifies the zones, applies sensitivity labels and collects lineage from Data Factory and Fabric pipelines and from Databricks Unity Catalog, so the lineage graph is emitted, not drawn.
  3. Rights ledger. A Delta table keyed by tenant and source: rights basis, allowed uses, opt-out flag, effective dates. The curation job joins against it and keeps only rows whose allowed uses include training.
  4. PII. Presidio (open source, from Microsoft) or Azure AI Language PII detection in the curation job, custom recognisers for tax identifiers, keyed-hash tokens for identifiers that joins need, and a sampled residual-risk review per dataset version.
  5. Versions. Delta versions for tables; Azure ML data assets (name:version) for training snapshots; the content hash in the card; MLflow logs the data asset version on every run, which is the edge from dataset to model.
  6. Feature pipelines. Bronze, silver and gold layers on Databricks or Fabric; a feature store with point-in-time joins so training and serving read the same definitions; Event Hubs with Spark Structured Streaming for features that must be minutes fresh.
  7. Deletion. A request is resolved through the ledger and lineage: delete from landing and curated, mark affected dataset versions, retrain or retire affected models on a published cadence, and record what was done.

Worked example: one quarter of categorization approvals illustrative

StepRowsNote

after the rights filter1,104,0008% of rows from tenants without a training basis or opted out

How training data gets the company into trouble

Bad“We have the data, so we can train on it.”
GoodA rights basis per record, default no, decided with Legal and enforced by a join.
BadScrubbing PII after a model has trained on it.
GoodPII handled before the training zone; a model cannot be relied on to forget.
BadTraining from a mutable table someone keeps “fixing”.
GoodImmutable snapshots with content hashes; a fix is a new version.
BadLineage documented in a wiki.
GoodLineage emitted by the pipelines into the catalogue.
BadA random split that puts one tenant’s products on both sides.
GoodSplits by tenant or time, with a leakage test.
BadSynthetic rows mixed in unlabelled.
GoodSynthetic rows labelled with the generator, its prompt version and the teacher’s terms.
BadFeatures computed one way for training and another for serving.
GoodOne feature definition with point-in-time joins, served from the same store.

A curation job: rights filter, redaction, tokens, card, registration

import hashlib, hmac, json, pandas as pd
from presidio_analyzer import AnalyzerEngine, PatternRecognizer, Pattern
from presidio_anonymizer import AnonymizerEngine
from presidio_anonymizer.entities import OperatorConfig

analyzer, anonymizer = AnalyzerEngine(), AnonymizerEngine()
analyzer.registry.add_recognizer(PatternRecognizer(                # tax ids are not in the default set
    supported_entity="US_EIN", patterns=[Pattern("ein", r"\b\d{2}-\d{7}\b", 0.6)]))

def redact(text: str) -> str:
    found = analyzer.analyze(text=text, language="en")
    return anonymizer.anonymize(text=text, analyzer_results=found,
        operators={"DEFAULT": OperatorConfig("replace", {"new_value": "<PII>"})}).text

def token(value: str, key: bytes) -> str:                     # joinable, not reversible without the key
    return hmac.new(key, value.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()[:16]

events = pd.read_parquet("curated/approvals/2026-q3/")        # one row per analyst approval or correction
ledger = pd.read_parquet("governance/rights_ledger/")         # tenant_id, source, allowed_uses, opted_out
ok = ledger[(ledger.source == "categorization") & ~ledger.opted_out
            & ledger.allowed_uses.apply(lambda uses: "train" in uses)]
rows = events.merge(ok[["tenant_id"]], on="tenant_id", how="inner")   # no basis, no row
rows["description"] = rows["description"].map(redact)
rows["tenant_ref"] = rows.pop("tenant_id").map(lambda t: token(t, KEY))   # KEY from Key Vault
rows = rows.drop_duplicates(subset=["description", "approved_category"])

path = "training/taxcat/v7/train.parquet"
rows.to_parquet(path, index=False)
digest = hashlib.sha256(open(path, "rb").read()).hexdigest()
card = {"name": "taxcat-train", "version": 7, "sha256": digest, "rows": len(rows),
        "sources": [{"system": "categorization-approvals", "from": "2026-07-01", "to": "2026-09-30"}],
        "rights_basis": "contract: service improvement; opt-outs excluded (ledger 2026-10-01)",
        "pii": {"scanner": "presidio + US_EIN", "free_text": "replace", "tenant_id": "HMAC-SHA256 token"},
        "splits": "by tenant 80/10/10", "retention_days": 730, "owner": "team-categorization"}
json.dump(card, open("training/taxcat/v7/dataset_card.json", "w"), indent=2)

# register the snapshot; every training run logs this name:version, which is the lineage edge to the model
from azure.ai.ml.entities import Data
from azure.ai.ml.constants import AssetTypes
ml.data.create_or_update(Data(name="taxcat-train", version="7", type=AssetTypes.URI_FOLDER,
                              path="azureml://datastores/training/paths/taxcat/v7/",
                              tags={"sha256": digest, "card": "dataset_card.json"}))

In the room

How would you set standards for training data from our AI products?Nothing trains without a dataset card: where the data came from, the rights basis and allowed uses, what PII was removed and how, how it was split, and its content hash. Customer data trains nothing by default; a rights ledger agreed with Legal says which tenants and sources may, and the curation job enforces it with a join, so the policy cannot be skipped. Every training run logs the dataset version, which gives us lineage from an approval click to a model behind an alias.
How do you handle PII?Before the training zone, never after. Typed masking for names and contacts in free text, dropped fields for tax identifiers and bank details, keyed-hash tokens for the identifiers we need for joins and tenant splits, and a sampled residual-risk review on every dataset version. Free text we cannot clean reliably stays out.
A customer asks to be deleted. What happens to the models?The ledger and the lineage graph tell us every record, every dataset version and every model touched. We delete the records, mark the dataset versions, and retrain or retire the affected models on a published cadence, because a model cannot be relied on to forget. Tokenised identifiers and tenant splits keep that blast radius small.
How would you architect the feature pipelines?Medallion layers on Databricks or Fabric, a feature store with point-in-time joins so training and serving share one definition, streaming through Event Hubs and Spark for anything that must be fresh in minutes, and lineage emitted into Purview. I have built that stack on Azure at E.ON and at streaming scale with Kafka and Spark at Telefónica.

6 · The central AI system: orchestration and abstraction layers

The central AI system is a stack of layers, each hiding one kind of change from the teams above it. The SDK hides transport and telemetry; the gateway hides identity, quotas and safety; aliases hide which model, provider and region; retrieve hides indexes; MCP hides tool implementations; the agent runtime hides where and how an agent runs. Each layer is a contract with a guarantee, and together they let a product team bring its own framework and still get the same safety, cost control and traces as everyone else.

From the job descriptionArchitect the orchestration and abstraction layers of the central AI system that connect LLMs to tools, data, and sub-agents … (and) establish reference architectures, paved-road patterns, and enterprise technical standards for agentic orchestration.
workflow or agent
code decides the steps where they are known; a model decides only where the path is open
runtime guarantees
an identity per agent · step, cost and time budgets · traces · durable state · governed tools · approvals
sub-agents
co-locate when they share a workflow and state; split over A2A for independent scale, a security boundary or reuse
frameworks
bless two (Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph); host any that honours the contracts

One request through the layers: the runtime is the hub, the gateway sees every hop

The layers, what each hides, and what it guarantees

LayerWhat teams callWhat it hidesGuarantee
SDKai.chat(alias, …), ai.retrieve(…), agent helpersTransport, retries, auth, trace propagationOne way to call; telemetry for free
gatewayAn OpenAI-compatible endpointIdentity, quotas, safety screening, caching, meteringNo call goes unaccounted
aliaseschat-default, chat-small, chat-reasoning, embed-v2Model version, provider, region, reserved or pay-as-you-goRemap and roll back without a code change
retrievalretrieve(query, filters, k) → passages with citationsIndexes, embeddings, chunking, entitlementsTrimming before ranking; a freshness SLO
toolsMCP servers registered behind the gatewayImplementation and back-end credentialsLeast privilege; every call logged
agent runtimerun(task, session) with budgets and approvalsHost (Agent Service or Container Apps), framework, checkpointingAn identity per agent; durable runs; enforced budgets
agent interopA2A agent cards and tasksWhere another agent runs and who owns itIdentity, quota and logging at the gateway

Workflow, agent, or both

Workflow

The steps are known; code orders them and a model fills in the language-shaped parts. Testable, cheap, predictable. The default for anything a tax engine already computes.

Agent

The path is open: which records to read, which rule applies, what to ask next. A model chooses the next step inside budgets the runtime enforces.

Workflow with agentic steps

The common production shape: a fixed outer process (detect, propose, validate, approve, apply) with an agent inside one or two steps.

Supervisor and specialists

One planner delegates to narrow agents with narrow tools. Co-located while they share state; split over A2A when one needs its own scale, boundary or other callers.

You have built supervisors, specialists and the backends under them

  • Capital Group. “Production GenAI systems with LangChain, MCP and multi-LLM orchestration, structured outputs and HITL review.” resume A supervisor and specialist sub-agents in one Bedrock AgentCore runtime; Kong in front of every model call; the split into separate runtimes over a gateway and MCP documented as the upgrade path. your account
  • Noctal. “Architected an end-to-end agentic AI platform (LangGraph, Pinecone, prompt optimization, HITL review) plus the Python/FastAPI backend and model-serving infrastructure”, with a Dialogflow CX conversational layer and “webhook fulfillment to FastAPI”. resume
  • Virtual Minds. “Agentic and RAG workflows with LangGraph, MCP, AWS Bedrock and pgvector.” resume
  • Xiom.AI. “Agent-based multi-LLM workflows for inventory planning, forecasting, pricing and replenishment.” resume
  • Protocols. A2A and ADK in your cloud-delivery line; MCP across three engagements. resume
How it transfersMicrosoft Agent Framework is to Azure what LangGraph and AgentCore are in your current work: a loop, tools, sessions and tracing. Foundry Agent Service is the managed runtime; Container Apps is the self-hosted path. The guarantees (identity, budgets, approvals, durable state, governed tools) are the ones you already enforce.
Say it before they doAgent Framework and Foundry Agent Service are study, not production. Show the code you would write (Code tab) and name what you would verify in week one: hosted-agent identities, the standard-setup bindings, and the status of the approval and long-running-agent previews.

The layers on Azure

  1. SDK. A thin, versioned package: the Azure OpenAI client pointed at the gateway with an Entra token, the alias as the deployment name, retrieve, and the agent helpers (budgets, approvals, untrusted-data labels). Consumer-driven contract tests run in the platform’s pipeline.
  2. Gateway. API Management with the AI-gateway policies: Entra token validation, an alias allow-list, managed identity to Foundry, token limits and metrics, Content Safety, semantic cache (card 12). It also exposes REST APIs as MCP servers, passes through remote MCP servers, and imports A2A endpoints.
  3. Runtime. Foundry Agent Service on the standard setup, so threads live in your Cosmos DB (at least 3,000 RU/s), files in your Storage and vector stores in your AI Search; the bindings cannot change on an existing project, so projects come from a template. Hosted agents in Agent Framework or LangGraph run as containers with their own Entra identity. Container Apps is the self-hosted path, with checkpoints in Cosmos DB.
  4. Tools. Every tool is an MCP server registered behind the gateway; Agent Service toolboxes point at the gateway’s MCP endpoints, never at the systems directly (card 7).
  5. Sub-agents. In-process for a shared workflow; separate hosted agents over A2A (v1.0 in Agent Service) for independent scaling, a security boundary or reuse.
  6. Approvals and durability. The approval primitive is part of your contract today; Foundry’s long-running hosted agents and approval step (preview, August 2026) are adopted behind it when they reach general availability.
  7. Traces. Agent Framework emits OpenTelemetry GenAI spans into Application Insights; with the gateway’s diagnostics in the same resource, one operation id spans gateway, runtime, tools and models.

Worked example: a configuration agent in an ERP illustrative design

A setting like Vertex’s Configuration Agent for Microsoft Dynamics 365, which detects changes such as new entities, registrations or locations and applies the tax configuration they need Vertex announcement, 25 Nov 2025. A workflow outside, an agent inside one step:

StepDecided byTool or serviceGuard
1 · detect a new legal entitycodeERP change eventidempotency key per event
2 · find the rules that applyspecialist agentretrieve over registration rulescitations required; tool output untrusted
3 · propose a change setsupervisor agentMCP: erp_entity_get, taxengine_config_previewstep and cost budget
4 · validatetax engineMCP: taxengine_config_validatedeterministic; the model cannot override it
5 · approvea tax analystapproval inboxdiff, citations and validation shown

How the central system goes wrong

BadTeams call model endpoints directly with keys in configuration.
GoodOnly the gateway’s managed identity can reach Foundry; teams hold Entra tokens for the gateway.
BadOne mandated framework for every team.
GoodTwo blessed frameworks with templates; any framework that honours the contracts can be hosted.
BadAn agent loop for a process whose steps are known.
GoodA workflow with agentic steps where the path is genuinely open.
BadA runtime per agent from day one: more hops, more cost, state passed over the network.
GoodCo-located specialists; split when scale, a boundary or reuse demands it.
BadBudgets written into the prompt.
GoodBudgets enforced by the runtime: steps, cost and wall-clock time, with a clean stop.
BadAgent state in process memory, lost on restart or during a two-day approval wait.
GoodCheckpoints in Cosmos DB; a run resumes where it stopped.
BadAn abstraction so tight that teams route around it to reach a new model feature.
GoodCapability flags on aliases and a pass-through mode that still goes through the gateway.

A supervisor with a specialist, governed tools and an approval, in Agent Framework

# pip install agent-framework-foundry azure-identity   (package and class names as documented in Oct 2026; check before use)
from agent_framework import Agent
from agent_framework.foundry import FoundryChatClient
from azure.identity import ManagedIdentityCredential

from aiplatform.agents import budgeted, requires_approval, untrusted   # platform SDK helpers
from aiplatform.tools import retrieve, mcp_tools                     # governed retrieval; MCP tools via the gateway

client = FoundryChatClient(project_endpoint=PROJECT_ENDPOINT, model="chat-default",   # an alias
                           credential=ManagedIdentityCredential())

rules_reader = Agent(client=client, name="registration-rules",
    instructions="Find the registration and filing rules that apply to the entity. Cite every rule.",
    tools=[untrusted(retrieve)])                               # retrieved text is data, never instructions

@requires_approval(blast_radius="external")                  # the run pauses until an analyst approves
async def apply_tax_config(entity_id: str, change_set: dict) -> str:
    """Apply an approved, validated tax-configuration change set."""
    ...

async def read_rules(entity_id: str) -> str:
    """Delegate to the rules specialist and return cited findings."""
    return (await rules_reader.run(f"Which rules apply to entity {entity_id}?")).text

supervisor = Agent(client=client, name="config-supervisor",
    instructions=("Propose tax-configuration changes for new entities. Validate every proposal with "
                  "taxengine_config_validate before asking to apply it. Never apply without cited findings."),
    tools=[read_rules, *mcp_tools("erp", "taxengine"), apply_tax_config])

@budgeted(max_steps=12, max_cost_usd=0.50, timeout_s=300)       # enforced by the runtime, not the prompt
async def handle(event: dict, session_id: str) -> str:
    session = supervisor.create_session(session_id)               # thread state in the platform's Cosmos DB
    return (await supervisor.run(f"New entity event: {event}", session=session)).text
# what a product team writes to call a model: nothing about keys, regions or providers
from aiplatform import ai

answer = ai.chat("chat-small", messages=msgs, schema=CategoryProposal,   # structured output is a contract too
                 workload="product-categorization")                  # attribution for quotas and showback

The four helpers are the difference between a demo and a production agent: budgeted stops runaway loops, requires_approval turns a tool into an interrupt with a recorded decision, untrusted keeps retrieved and tool text from acting as instructions, and mcp_tools only ever returns tools registered behind the gateway.

In the room

How would you architect the central AI system?As layers, each hiding one kind of change. The SDK hides transport and telemetry, the gateway hides identity, quotas and safety, aliases hide the model and provider, retrieve hides the indexes, MCP hides tool implementations, and the agent runtime hides where an agent runs while guaranteeing it an identity, budgets, durable state, traces and an approval step. Model calls and tool calls both pass the gateway, so there is one place for policy and one trace per request. On Azure that is API Management, Foundry, AI Search, MCP servers behind API Management, and Foundry Agent Service, with Container Apps as the self-hosted path.
Workflow or agent?Code decides wherever the steps are known; a model decides only where the path is genuinely open. In a tax business the engine computes and the model plans and explains, so most production shapes are a workflow with one or two agentic steps, and a deterministic validation the model cannot override.
How do you let teams use their own frameworks without chaos?The contracts are framework-neutral. Agent Framework and LangGraph are blessed with templates; any framework that calls models through the gateway, gets tools from the registry, emits OpenTelemetry and uses the approval primitive can be hosted. At Capital Group, Kong sits in front of every model call and Langfuse traces every step whichever library made it; that is the property I would keep.
One runtime with sub-agents, or a runtime per agent?Co-locate when the agents share a workflow and state: fewer hops, lower cost, simpler state. Split over A2A when one needs independent scale, a separate security boundary, or other callers. I made that call on AgentCore and wrote the split down as the upgrade path rather than paying for it on day one.

7 · MCP servers and the tool surface

Every tool definition is paid for on every call, and every extra tool is one more wrong choice the model can make. The tool surface is a design object with a budget: how many tools one model sees at the start of a turn, how many operations one MCP server exposes, and the point at which a domain stops being a handful of tools and becomes a specialist agent with its own instructions. The published numbers agree well enough to set standards from them.

From the job description… set standards for MCP servers, tool-surface design (optimal number of tools exposed per LLM and APIs per server), and when to use specialized sub-agents versus direct tool exposure.
per model
3–5 tools always loaded, under about 20 visible at the start of a turn; beyond that, tool search or a sub-agent
per server
one bounded context (tax engine, catalogue, ERP) with 5–15 task-shaped tools, never one per endpoint
sub-agent when
the domain needs its own instructions, more than about 15 tools, a different model, or its own security boundary
every server ships with
namespaced names, strict schemas, concise outputs with names and IDs, pagination, actionable errors, a read/write split, eval cases

Tools cost tokens before the conversation starts, so the surface needs layers

The rules, and the evidence behind each

RuleEvidence
Fewer than about 20 tools visible to a model at the start of a turnOpenAI’s function-calling guide: aim for fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn, “a soft suggestion”; use tool search and namespaces for larger surfaces OpenAI docs, Oct 2026
Defer the rest behind tool search once definitions pass about 10K tokens or 10 tools; keep the 3–5 most used loadedAnthropic: 58 tools ≈ 55K tokens; tool search raised MCP-evaluation accuracy from 49% to 74% (Opus 4) and 79.5% to 88.1% (Opus 4.5) and cut tool tokens by about 85% Anthropic, 24 Nov 2025
Retrieve tool descriptions instead of listing them allRAG-MCP: tool-selection accuracy 43.13% against 13.62% with every tool in the prompt, with about half the prompt tokens; in its stress test failures dominate once the right tool sits beyond roughly 100 positions arXiv 2505.03275, May 2025
Consolidate operations that are always called togetherOpenAI: “combine functions that are always called in sequence”; Anthropic: schedule_event instead of list_users, list_events and create_event Anthropic, 11 Sep 2025
Namespace by service and resourceAnthropic’s prefixes (asana_search, jira_search); OpenAI’s namespaces for deferred tools
Return meaningful, concise results; cap their sizeAnthropic: names over opaque IDs, a concise mode at about a third of the tokens, and Claude Code’s default cap of 25,000 tokens per tool response

Specialist sub-agent or direct tools

SignalDirect toolsSpecialist sub-agent
Tools in the domainup to about 10more than about 15, or growing
Instructions neededthe tool descriptions sufficedomain rules, a procedure, worked examples
Modelthe caller’s model fitsa cheaper or different model fits better
Securitysame identity and dataits own identity, data scope or approval rules
Contextresults are smallresults are large and only a summary should return
Latencytightcan afford one more model hop
Reuseone callerother applications want it (then expose it over A2A)

The MCP server standard

  1. One bounded context per server, the server name as the tool prefix: taxengine_quote, taxengine_config_validate.
  2. Task-shaped tools, 5–15 per server; consolidate sequences; never wrap every REST endpoint one to one.
  3. Strict schemas: enums for closed sets, unambiguous parameter names (entity_id, not id), descriptions written for a new analyst.
  4. Reads and writes separated; writes take an idempotency key and declare their blast radius so the runtime can require approval.
  5. Outputs concise by default with a detail option, names alongside IDs, pagination, and a size cap.
  6. Errors that say how to fix the call, never a bare status code.
  7. Auth: Entra at the gateway, on-behalf-of the user when the tool acts as the user, no token passthrough (forbidden by the MCP authorization spec since 2025-06-18); spec revision pinned (2025-11-25 or 2026-07-28).
  8. An evaluation set of 30–50 tasks with the expected tool calls, gated in CI on tool-call accuracy.

You have shipped MCP in production and designed the tool contracts

  • Virtual Minds. “Agentic and RAG workflows with LangGraph, MCP, AWS Bedrock and pgvector.” resume
  • Noctal. The Dialogflow CX layer with “webhook fulfillment to FastAPI”: tool contracts by another name, with schemas, timeouts and errors. resume

Why this card matters in the roomThe tool-count question in the job description is new for everyone. A principled answer with published numbers (the vendors’ ceilings, the token cost per server, the measured effect of tool search) and a decision table for sub-agents is rarer than experience with MCP itself.
Offer, do not claimYou have no published benchmark of your own on tool counts. Offer to build one in the first month: a tool-selection evaluation on Vertex’s real tool catalogue at 10, 20, 40 and 80 visible tools, so the standard rests on their models and their tools.

Building and governing the tool surface on Azure

  1. Inventory the APIs per domain (tax engine, catalogue, ERP connectors, content) and group them into bounded contexts: one MCP server each.
  2. Design task-shaped tools, write their descriptions as you would brief a new analyst, and draft the evaluation tasks at the same time.
  3. Implement with the MCP Python SDK on Container Apps or Functions, or let API Management expose an existing REST API as an MCP server without new code.
  4. Register behind the gateway: Entra authentication, rate limits per agent identity, logging of every call. Agent Service toolboxes point at the gateway’s MCP endpoints, so curation, auth and versioning live in one place.
  5. Budget each agent’s surface: count tools and definition tokens at the start of a turn; above 20 tools or 10K tokens, add tool search where the model supports it, or split a domain into a specialist.
  6. Gate on tool selection: ToolCallAccuracyEvaluator from azure-ai-evaluation on each agent’s task set, in CI.
  7. Version and retire: semantic versions per server, a deprecation window, usage per tool from gateway logs to find the ones nobody calls.

Worked example: how many tools should the configuration agent see? illustrative results; run it on the real catalogue
