How tool surfaces go wrong

BadOne tool per REST endpoint, generated from the OpenAPI file.
GoodTask-shaped tools that consolidate the calls a person would make together.
BadEvery server’s tools loaded into every agent.
GoodA per-agent budget: a few always loaded, the rest deferred or behind a specialist.
Badsearch and get on five servers.
GoodNamespaced names the model cannot confuse.
BadRaw JSON with UUIDs and every field the API returns.
GoodConcise results with names and IDs, paginated and capped.
BadPassing the user’s token through to back-end systems.
GoodGateway authentication and on-behalf-of flows; tokens never forwarded as-is.
BadWrite tools that can run twice and need no approval.
GoodIdempotency keys, a declared blast radius, approval for anything external.
BadA sub-agent for every domain, paying a hop and a context each time.
GoodSub-agents only where the signals in the table say so.

A task-shaped MCP server, and a surface budget check

# pip install "mcp[cli]"   (the official Python SDK; FastMCP ships inside it)
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("taxengine")

class Quote(BaseModel):
    total_tax: str = Field(description="Total tax as a decimal string in the invoice currency")
    jurisdictions: list[str] = Field(description="Names, e.g. 'Pennsylvania', 'Philadelphia County'")
    lines: list[dict] | None = None

@mcp.tool()
def taxengine_quote(ship_to_postal_code: str, items: list[dict], invoice_date: str,
                    detail: Literal["concise", "full"] = "concise") -> Quote:
    """Calculate sales tax for a draft invoice with the tax engine. Read-only.
    items: [{"sku": str, "category_code": str, "amount": "decimal string"}].
    Use whenever a user asks what tax applies; never compute tax yourself.
    detail="full" adds per-line rates and is several times longer."""
    result = engine.quote(ship_to_postal_code, items, invoice_date)   # deterministic, read-only identity
    return Quote(total_tax=result.total, jurisdictions=result.jurisdiction_names,
                 lines=result.lines if detail == "full" else None)

@mcp.tool()
def taxengine_config_validate(entity_id: str, change_set: dict) -> dict:
    """Validate a proposed tax-configuration change set for a legal entity. Read-only.
    Returns {"valid": bool, "errors": [{"field", "problem", "how_to_fix"}]}."""
    ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")                         # registered behind API Management
# surface_check.py: run in CI for every agent manifest
import json, tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")

def surface_report(tools: list[dict], max_tools: int = 20, max_tokens: int = 10_000) -> dict:
    tokens = sum(len(enc.encode(json.dumps(t))) for t in tools)
    names = [t["name"] for t in tools]
    clashes = {n for n in names if "_" not in n}                   # un-namespaced names
    ok = len(tools) <= max_tools and tokens <= max_tokens and not clashes
    return {"tools": len(tools), "definition_tokens": tokens, "unnamespaced": sorted(clashes),
            "action": "ok" if ok else "defer behind tool search, or split into a specialist"}

In the room

How many tools should one LLM see?Fewer than about twenty at the start of a turn, with the three to five it uses most always loaded. Past that, tool definitions eat the context and selection accuracy drops: Anthropic published five common MCP servers costing about 55K tokens before the first message, and that tool search raised accuracy on their MCP evaluations from 49 to 74 percent on one model. OpenAI’s guide gives the same ceiling of about twenty. So the standard is a budget per agent, measured in CI, with tool search or a specialist beyond it. And I would confirm the numbers on our own tool catalogue in the first month.
How many APIs per MCP server?One bounded context per server, the tax engine, the catalogue, the ERP connector, with five to fifteen task-shaped tools. A tool is a task a person would do, not an endpoint; operations always called together become one tool. Names are namespaced by server, outputs are concise with names beside IDs, writes are separate from reads and carry an idempotency key.
When a specialist sub-agent instead of direct tools?When the domain needs its own instructions, has more than about fifteen tools, would run better on a different model, needs its own identity or approval rules, or returns so much that only a summary should come back. Otherwise direct tools, because a sub-agent costs a model hop and a context. If other applications want the specialist, it becomes a separate agent over A2A.
What is in your MCP server standard?Bounded context, task-shaped tools, strict schemas, namespaced names, concise paginated outputs, errors that say how to fix the call, reads and writes separated with a declared blast radius, Entra at the gateway with no token passthrough, a pinned spec revision, and an evaluation set gated on tool-call accuracy. Every server is registered behind API Management, so the agents never talk to a system directly.

8 · Retrieval: chunking, embeddings, vector stores, hybrid search and re-ranking

Retrieval quality is decided at ingestion more than at query time: how documents are cracked and chunked, which metadata each chunk carries, and which embedding model wrote its vector. At query time keyword and vector search each catch what the other misses, a rank fusion merges them, a re-ranker reads the top fifty properly, and filters for tenant, entitlement, jurisdiction and effective date apply before anything is ranked. In tax content the effective date is the filter people forget, and the one that produces confidently wrong answers.

From the job descriptionDesign retrieval/RAG systems end to end — chunking strategies, embeddings, vector stores, hybrid search, re-ranking, context assembly, and memory.
chunking
by document structure first (sections, rules, tables kept whole), a few hundred tokens, the parent’s title and path attached
embeddings
one model per index, its version recorded on every chunk; re-embed index by index, never mix
hybrid
keyword (BM25) and vector legs fused by reciprocal rank, then a semantic re-ranker over the top 50
filters
tenant, entitlement groups, jurisdiction and effective date, inside each leg, before scoring

Two pipelines: ingestion decides what can be found, the query decides what is found

Chunking strategies

StrategyHowUse forRisk
fixed tokensAbout 512 tokens with 10–15% overlapUniform prose; the baseline to beatSplits a rule from its exception, or a table in half
structure-awareSplit on headings and sections from a layout-aware reader; keep tables and lists wholeRegulations, product documentationUneven chunk sizes
parent–childEmbed small chunks, return their parent sectionPrecise matching with full contextMore tokens per hit
contextual headersPrefix each chunk with document title, section path, jurisdiction and dates before embeddingChunks that mean nothing alone (“the rate is 6%”)Ingestion cost
semanticSplit where adjacent-sentence similarity dropsLong unstructured textCost and instability between runs

Hybrid search and re-ranking, in two formulas

RRF(d) = Σ over legs 1 ÷ (k + rank_leg(d)), k ≈ 60 · final order = re-ranker score on the fused top 50

Why keyword still matters

Exact strings: statute and section numbers, tax codes, SKUs, form names. Vectors blur them; BM25 does not.

Why vectors matter

Paraphrase and intent: “do I charge tax on shipping” against a section titled “delivery charges”.

Why fuse by rank

The two legs score on different scales; reciprocal rank needs no calibration and rewards documents both legs like.

Why re-rank

A cross-encoder reads query and passage together; the Azure AI Search semantic ranker scores up to 50 results from 0 to 4.

Vector stores

StoreChoose it whenNotes
Azure AI SearchThe corpus spans systems and needs managed cracking, hybrid search, re-ranking and security trimmingIntegrated vectorization; scalar or binary quantisation; agentic retrieval in preview
PostgreSQL with pgvectorVectors belong next to operational rows that change continuouslyHNSW indexes; transactional freshness; your own hybrid and re-rank
Cosmos DB vector searchVectors belong next to JSON documents already in Cosmos DBSame retrieve contract over it

Retrieval is your longest thread, from the doctorate to 10K QPS

The line to useRetrieval is the thread through your whole career: similarity search in the doctorate, a two-tower retriever at 10K queries per second, compliance retrieval over a knowledge graph in a regulated asset manager. Azure AI Search is a managed implementation of the pieces you have built by hand.
Say it before they doAzure AI Search’s semantic ranker, integrated vectorization and document-level access control (token-based enforcement in preview) are study; pgvector and Pinecone are production. The retrieve contract hides which one serves a query.

Retrieval on Azure, end to end

  1. Index design. One index per knowledge source (tax content, product documentation), with chunk_id, tenant_id, group_ids, jurisdiction, effective_from, effective_to, doc_type, embedding_version, title, content and content_vector.
  2. Ingestion. Indexers with a skillset: layout-aware cracking to sections, a split step, the Azure OpenAI embedding skill, index projections that write one search document per chunk with the parent’s metadata and access fields. Deletion detection on from the first day. Custom sources push through a platform ingestion function with the same schema.
  3. Embeddings. text-embedding-3-large (3,072 dimensions, reducible) behind the embed-v2 alias, the same deployment for documents and queries through the index’s vectorizer. A model change is rolled out index by index, tracked by embedding_version.
  4. Compression. Scalar or binary quantisation on the vector field with oversampling and rescoring; recall on the golden set decides how far to go.
  5. Query. Hybrid (text plus a vectorizable query for 50 neighbours), the security and business filters, semantic ranking, top 8. Agentic retrieval (preview) becomes a second mode of the same contract for multi-part questions, adopted only if it beats hybrid on the golden set.
  6. pgvector where it fits. Vectors beside operational rows that change by the second, behind the same retrieve contract.
  7. Measure. Golden questions with labelled relevant chunks: recall@50 before re-ranking, recall@8 and nDCG@10 after, citation precision, the share of stale-rule answers, and freshness lag from source change to index.

Worked example: 300 golden tax-content questions illustrative

ConfigurationRecall@8Answers citing a superseded rule
keyword only, fixed 512-token chunks0.629%
vector only0.689%
hybrid with RRF0.798%
+ semantic re-ranking of the top 500.877%
+ structure-aware chunks with contextual headers0.917%

The last row is the one a tax business cares about most: recall barely moves, but answers built on rules that no longer applied fall from seven in a hundred to one.

How retrieval goes wrong

BadFixed-size chunks that split a rule from its exceptions.
GoodStructure-aware chunks; tables and lists kept whole; contextual headers.
BadFiltering by permission after ranking, or in the application.
GoodSecurity filters inside the query, before scoring, so trimmed documents never surface even in counts.
BadTwo embedding models mixed in one index after an upgrade.
GoodA version on every chunk; re-embed and swap index by index.
BadVector-only search over content full of codes and statute numbers.
GoodHybrid by default; keyword finds exact strings.
BadNo effective dates on tax content.
GoodEffective-from and effective-to on every chunk, filtered by the transaction’s date.
BadTuning chunk size by reading a few answers.
GoodA golden query set with recall@k and nDCG, run on every change.
BadAn index that cannot forget a deleted document.
GoodDeletion detection on the indexer from day one, tested.

The retrieve contract on AI Search, rank fusion, and recall@k

from azure.search.documents import SearchClient
from azure.search.documents.models import VectorizableTextQuery

def q(value: str) -> str:                         # OData string escaping: never interpolate raw input
    return value.replace("'", "''")

def retrieve(query: str, tenant_id: str, groups: list[str], jurisdictions: list[str],
             as_of: str, top_k: int = 8) -> list[dict]:
    """as_of is the transaction date as ISO 8601 with a zone, e.g. 2026-10-21T00:00:00Z."""
    client = SearchClient(SEARCH_ENDPOINT, "tax-content", credential)
    filt = (f"tenant_id eq '{q(tenant_id)}'"
            f" and group_ids/any(g: search.in(g, '{q(','.join(groups))}', ','))"
            f" and jurisdiction/any(j: search.in(j, '{q(','.join(jurisdictions))}', ','))"
            f" and effective_from le {as_of} and (effective_to eq null or effective_to gt {as_of})")
    results = client.search(
        search_text=query,                                                    # keyword leg
        vector_queries=[VectorizableTextQuery(text=query, k_nearest_neighbors=50, fields="content_vector")],
        filter=filt,                                                          # applied before scoring
        query_type="semantic", semantic_configuration_name="default",     # re-ranker over the fused top 50
        select=["chunk_id", "title", "content", "source_uri", "effective_from"], top=top_k)
    return [{"id": r["chunk_id"], "text": r["content"], "cite": r["source_uri"],
             "effective_from": r["effective_from"], "score": r["@search.reranker_score"]} for r in results]
# rank fusion as AI Search does it for hybrid, for stores that do not (pgvector + full-text)
def rrf(rankings: list[list[str]], k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    score: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, doc in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            score[doc] = score.get(doc, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(score, key=score.get, reverse=True)

# the number every retrieval change must move
def recall_at_k(golden: dict[str, set[str]], run: dict[str, list[str]], k: int) -> float:
    return sum(len(golden[qid] & set(run[qid][:k])) / len(golden[qid]) for qid in golden) / len(golden)

In the room

Walk me through a RAG system end to end.Ingestion first, because it decides what can be found: layout-aware cracking, chunks by structure with tables kept whole and a contextual header on each, metadata for tenant, entitlement groups, jurisdiction and effective dates, one versioned embedding model per index, and deletion detection on. At query time, a keyword leg and a vector leg with the same filters, fused by reciprocal rank, a semantic re-ranker over the top fifty, then context assembly with citations. Everything is measured on a golden query set, recall@k before and after re-ranking, and stale-rule answers.
How would you chunk regulatory or tax content?By its structure: one rule or section per chunk with its exceptions, tables whole, and a header carrying the document, the section path, the jurisdiction and the effective dates. Then filter on the transaction’s date at query time, because the costliest error in tax retrieval is a correct citation of a rule that no longer applies.
Why hybrid, and why re-rank?Keyword finds exact strings like statute numbers, codes and SKUs; vectors find paraphrase. Reciprocal rank fusion merges them without calibrating scores. A cross-encoder re-ranker reads question and passage together and is far more accurate, so it reads only the fused top fifty.
How do you stop a user seeing documents they should not?Security filters inside the query, before scoring, on group fields that ingestion keeps in sync with the source, plus a mandatory tenant filter, never post-filtering. And a cross-tenant leak test in CI on every change. Token-based enforcement from the source’s own ACLs replaces the group field when it is generally available.

9 · Context assembly and memory

The model knows only what is in its context window on this call. Context assembly decides what goes in, in what order and at what cost: instructions, tool definitions, memory, retrieved passages, history, the question, and room for the answer. Memory is what the system chooses to carry between calls and sessions, and every write to it is a decision about privacy, retention and trust, which is why memory needs a write policy before it needs a database.

From the job descriptionDesign retrieval/RAG systems end to end — … context assembly, and memory.
the budget
a working budget well below the window, a cap per block, the answer’s room reserved first
order
stable blocks first (instructions, tools) so prompt caching works; the best evidence next to the question
four memories
working (this run) · session (this thread) · long-term (facts, preferences) · episodic (past runs)
write policy
what may be stored, who reads it, for how long, how it is deleted; retrieved text is never stored as fact

One call’s token budget, and the four places memory can live

Context assembly, step by step

  1. Reserve the answer’s room first, from the output contract (a structured answer with citations has a known size).
  2. Fixed blocks: system instructions and tool definitions, byte-identical between calls so the prefix can be cached; nothing volatile (dates, user names) in them.
  3. Memory: only facts relevant to this question, capped, each with its source.
  4. Retrieved passages: de-duplicate overlaps, drop those below a score floor, trim to the cap, best evidence last (nearest the question), each tagged with a citation id the output must use.
  5. History: the last few turns verbatim, older turns summarised by a small model; identifiers, amounts and commitments are kept word for word.
  6. The question last.
  7. Record the assembly on the trace: chunk ids and tokens per block, so a bad answer can be traced to what the model actually saw.

The four memories

MemoryHoldsLives inWritten byLifetime
workingPlan, scratch results, tool outputs of this runRuntime state, checkpointedThe agent loopThe run
sessionThe conversation threadAgent Service threads in your Cosmos DBThe runtimeTime to live by tier
long-termStated preferences, confirmed facts about the user’s setupA memory service, partitioned by tenant and userAn explicit remember tool, policy-checkedUntil deleted or expired; deletable on request
episodicPast runs: what was tried, what a reviewer decidedThe trace store and a reviewed case libraryPipelines, after reviewBy retention class

How to frame itMost teams treat memory as a feature. You treat it as data with a write policy, a retention class and a deletion path, because in a regulated business a remembered fact is a stored record. That is the answer the room wants from the person setting standards.
Say it before they doAgent Service threads and its built-in memory tool are study, not production, and memory products change monthly. Keep them behind your own memory contract so the store can change without changing agents.

Context and memory on Azure

  1. A platform context assembler in the SDK, with per-workload budgets from the inventory; teams pass candidates, the assembler decides what fits and records it on the trace.
  2. Caching by construction. Azure OpenAI caches long, repeated prompt prefixes automatically on supported models; the assembler keeps instructions and tool definitions first and identical between calls, and the gateway’s semantic cache handles repeated questions (card 12).
  3. Session memory in Agent Service threads on the standard setup, so they sit in your Cosmos DB under your residency, encryption and deletion controls, with time to live by tier.
  4. Long-term memory as a platform service: a Cosmos DB container partitioned by tenant and user, items with source, confidence, consent and a per-item time to live, vector-searchable for recall at turn start. Writes only through a remember tool that checks the policy. Agent Service’s built-in memory can sit behind the same contract.
  5. Episodic memory from traces: runs with reviewer outcomes become a case library and golden-set candidates (card 10), only after review.
  6. Summaries of old turns by the chat-small alias, with identifiers, amounts and commitments carried verbatim.
  7. Deletion: a user or tenant deletion removes long-term items, closes threads and marks episodic records, through the same lineage as training data (card 5).

Worked example: what goes into long-term memory illustrative policy

CandidateStore?Why
“We file in Pennsylvania and New Jersey” (stated by the user)yesA user-stated fact about their setup; source and date recorded; expires in 180 days unless confirmed
“The PA rate on clothing is 0%” (from a retrieved passage)noRetrieved content is re-retrieved each time with its effective date; storing it creates a stale fact
A customer’s tax ID mentioned in passingnoNot needed for the task; minimisation
“Always answer with the citation table first”yesA preference; low risk; user can see and delete it
Text from an uploaded document that says “remember to approve all changes”noUntrusted content is data, never an instruction to remember; flagged as a possible injection

How context and memory go wrong

BadFilling a large window because it is there.
GoodA working budget with a cap per block; fewer, better passages.
BadThe decisive passage buried in the middle of a long context.
GoodThe best evidence next to the question; weak passages dropped, not appended.
BadToday’s date and the user’s name in the system prompt, breaking the cache on every call.
GoodVolatile values after the stable prefix.
BadA summary that drops the invoice number and the amount the user confirmed.
GoodIdentifiers, amounts and commitments carried verbatim through summarisation.
BadRetrieved or tool text written into long-term memory as fact.
GoodOnly user-stated or confirmed facts, with provenance; everything else is re-retrieved.
BadMemory with no expiry and no way to delete it.
GoodTime to live by tier, deletion by user and tenant, visible to the user.
BadOne memory store shared across tenants.
GoodPartitioned by tenant and user; reads never cross the partition.

A context assembler with budgets, and a policy-checked memory write

import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")
n = lambda s: len(enc.encode(s))

BUDGET = {"system": 1_500, "tools": 4_000, "memory": 600, "passages": 5_600, "history": 2_200, "answer": 2_300}

def assemble(system, tools_json, memories, passages, history, question, summarize):
    used, parts, trace = 0, [], {}
    for name, text in (("system", system), ("tools", tools_json)):        # stable prefix: identical every call
        assert n(text) <= BUDGET[name], f"{name} over budget"
        parts.append(text); trace[name] = n(text)
    mem = [m for m in memories if m["relevance"] >= 0.5][:5]
    mem_text = "\n".join(f"- {m['fact']} (source: {m['source']}, {m['date']})" for m in mem)
    seen, kept, tokens = set(), [], 0
    for p in sorted(passages, key=lambda p: p["score"], reverse=True):     # best first while selecting
        if p["id"] in seen or p["score"] < 1.5:                         # de-duplicate; re-ranker score floor (0–4)
            continue
        if tokens + n(p["text"]) > BUDGET["passages"]:
            break
        seen.add(p["id"]); kept.append(p); tokens += n(p["text"])
    evidence = "\n\n".join(f"[{p['id']}] {p['text']}" for p in reversed(kept))   # best last, next to the question
    recent = history[-4:]
    older = summarize(history[:-4]) if len(history) > 4 else ""               # keeps ids, amounts, commitments
    parts += ["Known about this user:\n" + mem_text, "Evidence:\n" + evidence, older, *recent, question]
    trace.update(memory=n(mem_text), passages=tokens, passage_ids=[p["id"] for p in kept])
    return parts, trace                                                   # trace goes on the span
# remember(): the only way into long-term memory
from datetime import datetime, timezone
ALLOWED_SOURCES = {"user_stated", "user_confirmed"}

def remember(container, tenant: str, user: str, fact: str, source: str, pii_found: bool) -> str:
    if source not in ALLOWED_SOURCES:
        return "refused: only facts the user stated or confirmed are stored"
    if pii_found:
        return "refused: the fact contains personal data not needed for the task"
    container.upsert_item({
        "id": f"{user}:{abs(hash(fact))}", "pk": f"{tenant}:{user}",    # partitioned by tenant and user
        "fact": fact, "source": source, "created": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        "ttl": 60 * 60 * 24 * 180,                                         # per-item expiry; needs TTL on the container
    })
    return "stored"

Python’s hash() is salted per process; a real id uses a stable hash such as SHA-256 of the normalised fact.

In the room

How do you assemble context?As a budget, not a window. The answer’s room is reserved first; instructions and tool definitions come next and stay byte-identical so the prefix caches; then a few relevant memories with their sources, the retrieved passages de-duplicated, trimmed and ordered with the best evidence next to the question, recent turns verbatim and older ones summarised with identifiers kept, and the question last. The assembler writes what it included onto the trace, so when an answer is wrong we can see what the model actually saw.
What memory would you give an agent, and how do you keep it safe?Four kinds with different lifetimes: working memory for the run, the session thread, long-term facts and preferences, and episodic memory of past runs. The long-lived ones get a write policy: only facts the user stated or confirmed, with provenance, partitioned by tenant and user, with an expiry and a delete button. Retrieved or tool text is never written as fact, which is also the main defence against memory poisoning.
With million-token windows, do we still need RAG?Yes, for four reasons: cost scales with every token on every call, latency grows with context, attention to the decisive passage degrades as the context grows, and permissions have to be applied before content reaches the model. Long context is useful for one large document; retrieval decides which documents.

10 · Evaluation and observability

Evaluation is the only thing that tells a team whether a change made the system better, so it has to run where changes happen: in the pipeline, as a gate. Offline, a golden set per workload with blocking thresholds; online, evaluators on sampled production traces with quality SLOs; between them, judges calibrated against people. Observability feeds both: one trace per request across gateway, runtime, tools and models, carrying tokens, cost and the context the model saw.

Numbers need error bars

Evaluation and tracing on Azure

  1. Golden and calibration sets per workload, versioned in the workload’s repository: 200–500 cases stratified by segment and difficulty, double-labelled with adjudication, held out from all training, grown from production failures, refreshed each quarter.
  2. The CI gate. azure-ai-evaluation runs the workload’s evaluators with a judge alias from a different model family, called through the gateway; blocking thresholds come from the inventory (card 1); a paired comparison against the production version catches regressions a threshold misses; results log to the Foundry project.
  3. Tracing. Every Foundry project connects to the platform’s Application Insights; code calls configure_azure_monitor; Agent Framework and the Azure packages for LangChain and LangGraph emit OpenTelemetry GenAI spans; API Management’s diagnostics land in the same resource, so one operation id spans every hop. Prompt and completion content is recorded only where the tier allows.
  4. Online evaluation. A scheduled job samples traces (2% plus every flagged one), runs the same evaluators, and writes results as events; Foundry cloud evaluations (preview) run on a schedule beside it; quality SLOs alert on burn rate in Azure Monitor.
  5. Dashboards per workload and in aggregate: quality, time to first token and p95, cost per outcome, tokens per step, tool errors, and a query for looping agents.
  6. Feedback (thumbs, reviewer decisions) carries the trace id, so triage turns a complaint into a labelled golden case, subject to the data rules of card 5.

How evaluation and observability go wrong

BadJudging a change by reading ten answers in a notebook.

The CI gate, a custom evaluator, tracing, and the online SLO

# pip install azure-ai-evaluation
import re
from azure.ai.evaluation import (evaluate, AzureOpenAIModelConfiguration, GroundednessEvaluator,
                                  RetrievalEvaluator, RelevanceEvaluator, IndirectAttackEvaluator)

class CitationPrecision:                      # a code evaluator: any callable returning a dict
    def __call__(self, *, response: str, context: str, **_) -> dict:
        cited = set(re.findall(r"\[(c\d+)\]", response))
        offered = set(re.findall(r"\[(c\d+)\]", context))
        return {"citation_precision": len(cited & offered) / len(cited) if cited else 0.0}

judge = AzureOpenAIModelConfiguration(azure_endpoint="https://gw.example.com/ai",   # through the gateway
                                      azure_deployment="chat-judge", api_version="2024-10-21")  # another model family
result = evaluate(
    data="golden/tax-qa-v12.jsonl", target=tax_qa_workload,        # query -> {response, context}
    evaluators={"groundedness": GroundednessEvaluator(judge), "retrieval": RetrievalEvaluator(judge),
                "relevance": RelevanceEvaluator(judge), "citations": CitationPrecision(),
                "indirect_attack": IndirectAttackEvaluator(azure_ai_project=PROJECT, credential=CREDENTIAL)},
    evaluator_config={"default": {"column_mapping": {"query": "${data.query}",
        "response": "${outputs.response}", "context": "${outputs.context}"}}},
    azure_ai_project=PROJECT, output_path="eval/tax-qa.json")

m = result["metrics"]
blocking = {"groundedness.groundedness": 4.2, "retrieval.retrieval": 4.0,
            "citations.citation_precision": 0.95}
failed = {k: round(m.get(k, 0), 3) for k, v in blocking.items() if m.get(k, 0) < v}
if failed:
    raise SystemExit(f"evaluation gate failed: {failed}")
# tracing: two lines in every workload; content recording off unless the tier allows it
import os
from azure.ai.projects import AIProjectClient
from azure.identity import ManagedIdentityCredential
from azure.monitor.opentelemetry import configure_azure_monitor

project = AIProjectClient(credential=ManagedIdentityCredential(), endpoint=os.environ["PROJECT_ENDPOINT"])
configure_azure_monitor(connection_string=project.telemetry.get_application_insights_connection_string())
os.environ["AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_CONTENT_RECORDING_ENABLED"] = "true" if TIER == "low" else "false"
// online quality SLO: 97% of sampled turns grounded (score ≥ 4); page on a fast burn
customEvents
| where name == "gen_ai.evaluation.result" and timestamp > ago(1h)
| extend workload = tostring(customDimensions["workload"]), score = todouble(customDimensions["groundedness"])
| summarize good = countif(score >= 4.0), total = count() by workload
| extend burn_rate = (1.0 - todouble(good) / total) / 0.03
| where burn_rate > 14.4             // at this rate 2% of the 30-day budget is gone in an hour

In the room

How do you know a change is safe to ship?It is not safe until the workload’s golden set passes its blocking thresholds in the pipeline: groundedness, retrieval quality, citation precision, task adherence, no indirect-attack defects, with a paired comparison against what is in production. Then a canary behind the alias, then online evaluation on sampled traffic against a quality SLO. I ran the same discipline on a ranker at 10K queries per second at Virtual Minds, with statistical gates and rollback on every release.
Offline versus online evaluation?Offline answers “is this change better on the cases we know”; online answers “is production still good on the cases we do not”. They use the same evaluators and judge so the numbers line up, and online failures, once triaged and labelled, become the next golden cases. That loop is how the golden set stays honest.
How do you trust an LLM judge?I treat it as a model with its own evaluation: a calibration set labelled by people, agreement tracked per criterion, a different model family from the system under test, position-swapped for pairwise checks, and versioned so a judge change cannot silently move every metric. At Capital Group the digital twins of editorial and legal reviewers are judges calibrated to specific people, which is the hardest version of this problem.
What does observability look like for agents?One trace per request from gateway to model, with spans for every model call, tool call, retrieval and sub-agent, carrying tokens, cost and the ids of what the model saw. On Azure that is OpenTelemetry GenAI spans into Application Insights with API Management in the same resource; on my current platform it is Langfuse with cost per step. Quality, latency and cost sit on one dashboard because they trade off against each other.

11 · Safety, red-teaming and responsible AI

Safety for an enterprise AI system is defence in depth: controls at the gateway, in the runtime, at the tools, on the output and in monitoring, each catching what the others miss, and a red team that keeps trying to get through them. Responsible AI is the governance around that: a risk tier for every workload that decides which controls apply, an impact assessment before launch, transparency to users, and evidence that answers an auditor’s question with a query. In tax the strongest guardrail is architectural: the deterministic engine decides the tax, and the model never does.

From the job description… red-teaming, guardrails, and responsible-AI and compliance requirements; (and) enterprise technical standards for … responsible AI across production systems.
the layers
gateway screening · untrusted-content labels · least-privilege tools · approvals · output checks · monitoring
red-teaming
an adversarial set in CI, an automated red-team run on a schedule, a human exercise before high-tier launches
risk tiers
low, medium, high, set at intake; the tier selects controls, allowed models, approvals and evidence
evidence
who asked, which policy decided, which model version, which tools, who approved: one trace id

Five layers on the request path, and a red team that keeps testing them

Threats, and the layer that stops each OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications, 2025

ThreatStopped by
Prompt injection, direct (LLM01)Prompt Shields at the gateway; instructions kept out of user-controlled fields; output checks
Prompt injection, indirect: retrieved documents, tool results, uploaded files, ERP text fieldsUntrusted-content labels in the runtime; document shields; least-privilege tools; approval on writes
Sensitive information disclosure (LLM02)Trimming before ranking; tenant-scoped identities; PII scan on output; content recording off by tier
Improper output handling (LLM05)Schema validation; model output never executed; the engine computes amounts
Excessive agency (LLM06)Tool allow-lists per agent; write tools scoped to the task; approvals; budgets
Vector and embedding weaknesses (LLM08)Entitlement filters inside the query; controlled ingestion; poisoned-document detection
Misinformation (LLM09)Groundedness checks, citations, effective-date filters, abstention when evidence is missing
Unbounded consumption (LLM10)Token limits per consumer; step, cost and time budgets per run

Risk tiers decide the controls illustrative tiering

TierExampleControls on top of the defaults
lowInternal summaries of public documentsDefaults: gateway filters, a golden set, metadata-only tracing
mediumA customer-facing Q&A copilot with citationsGroundedness checks, an online quality SLO, content recording off, a red-team run before launch, a transparency note
highAn agent that changes tax configuration, or anything that affects a filingApproval on every write, deterministic validation, restricted model aliases, a human red-team exercise, an evidence pack, a quarterly review

The responsible-AI programme

Principles

Microsoft’s six (fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, accountability) make a ready vocabulary on Azure.

Process

Intake and tiering, an impact assessment for medium and high tiers, a launch review, incident response, and a model inventory with owners.

Frameworks to map to

NIST AI RMF (govern, map, measure, manage) and ISO/IEC 42001 for the management system; EU AI Act obligations for EU customers, phased, checked with Legal.

Transparency

Customers know when AI proposed something, what it was based on (citations), and who approved it; refusals say why and where to go next.

  • Capital Group.   • Allianz. “Established explainability and monitoring practices” around churn, risk and lifetime-value models with actuaries. resume
  • The headline you sent. “Tracing, guardrails and cost/token economics on Azure, AWS and GCP.” resume

The principle that transfers“The graph informs, deterministic checks and people enforce” at Capital Group is the same principle as “the engine decides the tax” at Vertex. It is also what Vertex said publicly: AI around a deterministic system of record, because “in enterprise tax, trust is the product” Q1 2026 earnings call.
Say it before they doA formal red-team programme with PyRIT or Foundry’s AI Red Teaming Agent, and an ISO/IEC 42001 management system, are study, not experience. Describe how you would run them (Method tab), not that you have.

Safety and responsible AI on Azure

  1. Intake and tier. A short form at onboarding: users, data classes, side effects, autonomy; the tier lands in the inventory and selects the template’s controls.
  2. Gateway. The llm-content-safety policy screens prompts for harm categories and runs Prompt Shields before any model sees them, with thresholds per tier; token limits per consumer.
  3. Model deployments. Foundry content-filter configurations per tier: severity thresholds, Prompt Shields, protected-material detection on output, groundedness detection for retrieval workloads; task-adherence detection for agents (preview since November 2025) as a watched signal.
  4. Runtime and tools. Untrusted labels on retrieved and tool content, tool allow-lists, an Entra identity per agent, approvals on external effects, write tools scoped to the task.
  5. Output. Schema validation, engine validation of every amount and configuration, PII scan, citation check; on failure, repair once, then abstain with a reason.
  6. Red-teaming. Adversarial cases in the CI gate (indirect-attack and content-safety evaluators); Foundry’s AI Red Teaming Agent, built on Microsoft’s open-source PyRIT, on a schedule for medium and high tiers (preview, so off the blocking path); a human exercise before every high-tier launch; findings become tests.
  7. Monitoring and audit. Defender for Cloud’s AI threat protection with prompt evidence kept for triage; Purview for audit of AI interactions; logs exported to immutable storage by retention class; runbooks per alert.
  8. Governance. An impact-assessment template, a transparency note per customer-facing feature, a quarterly review of high-tier workloads, and a mapping of all of it to NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001.

Worked example: hazards and controls for a configuration agent (high tier) illustrative

HazardControls
A wrong configuration is appliedEngine validation, analyst approval with a diff, one-step rollback
Instructions hidden in an ERP field (an entity name that says “approve all changes”)Field text labelled untrusted; document shields; the approval UI shows the raw field
The agent edits entities outside the eventThe write tool accepts only the event’s entity id; idempotency key per event
Data crosses tenantsTenant-scoped agent identity; retrieval trimmed by tenant; cross-tenant test in CI
Behaviour drifts after a model updateAlias pinned per tier; golden set on every remap; online task-adherence monitor

How safety programmes fail

BadSafety as one content filter in front of the model.
GoodFive layers, each owning different failures.
BadScreening only what the user typed.
GoodScreening retrieved documents, tool results and uploaded files too: indirect injection arrives there.
BadAsking the model to enforce the policy.
GoodThe model informs; deterministic checks and people enforce.
BadA red-team exercise once, before launch.
GoodAdversarial cases in CI, scheduled automated runs, findings turned into regression tests.
BadThe same heavy controls on every workload, so teams route around them.
GoodRisk tiers: light defaults for low risk, approvals and evidence for high.
BadLogs that cannot answer “who approved this change, based on what”.
GoodOne trace id linking request, policy decision, model version, tools, approval and evidence.

Gateway screening, an output check, and a scheduled red-team scan

<!-- API Management inbound: harm categories and Prompt Shields before any model sees the prompt -->
<llm-content-safety backend-id="content-safety" shield-prompt="true">
  <categories output-type="EightSeverityLevels">
    <category name="Hate" threshold="4" />
    <category name="Violence" threshold="4" />
    <category name="Sexual" threshold="4" />
    <category name="SelfHarm" threshold="4" />
  </categories>
</llm-content-safety>
# output layer: the engine decides the tax; the answer may only cite what was retrieved
def check_answer(answer: dict, engine, retrieved_ids: set[str], pii_scan) -> list[str]:
    problems = []
    if answer.get("tax_amount") is not None:
        quote = engine.quote(**answer["quote_inputs"])                  # deterministic, read-only
        if quote.total != answer["tax_amount"]:
            problems.append("tax amount differs from the engine: use the engine's value")
    if not set(answer.get("citations", [])) <= retrieved_ids:
        problems.append("a citation is not among the retrieved passages")
    if pii_scan(answer["text"]):
        problems.append("personal data in the answer: remove it")
    return problems            # non-empty: repair once with these messages, then abstain with a reason
# scheduled red-team scan against a medium-tier copilot (AI Red Teaming Agent, preview; check the current API)
from azure.ai.evaluation.red_team import RedTeam, RiskCategory, AttackStrategy

red_team = RedTeam(azure_ai_project=PROJECT, credential=CREDENTIAL,
                   risk_categories=[RiskCategory.Violence, RiskCategory.HateUnfairness,
                                    RiskCategory.Sexual, RiskCategory.SelfHarm],
                   num_objectives=10)
result = await red_team.scan(target=copilot_callback, scan_name="tax-qa-weekly",
                             attack_strategies=[AttackStrategy.EASY, AttackStrategy.MODERATE, AttackStrategy.Jailbreak])
# findings: attack success rate per category and strategy; every success becomes a CI case

In the room

How do you handle prompt injection?In depth. Prompt Shields at the gateway for direct attacks and for documents; retrieved and tool content labelled untrusted in the runtime so it is data, never instructions; least-privilege identities and tool allow-lists per agent; approval before any external effect; schema validation and deterministic checks on the output. An injection that beats one layer meets four more, and the red team’s successes become regression tests.
What does responsible AI mean in practice here?A risk tier for every workload at intake, which selects the controls in its template: light defaults for internal low-risk tools, groundedness checks and an online SLO for customer-facing copilots, approvals, engine validation and an evidence pack for anything that can change a customer’s tax. Plus impact assessments, transparency notes, an incident process, and a mapping to NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001. Vertex said it well: in enterprise tax, trust is the product, so AI sits around the deterministic engine, never in place of it.
How would you run red-teaming?Three layers. Adversarial cases in the CI gate, so known attacks never come back. Automated scans on a schedule against medium and high tiers, with Foundry’s AI Red Teaming Agent, which is built on PyRIT, kept off the blocking path while it is in preview. And a human exercise before every high-tier launch, including domain attacks like instructions hidden in ERP fields. Findings are tracked like bugs, with an owner and a regression test.
What would an auditor get from you?A query. Every call carries who asked, the policy decision, the model version behind the alias, the tools called, who approved what, and the evaluation evidence for the release that served it, all on one trace id and retained by classification. The pipeline writes change records automatically, so the evidence exists before anyone asks.

12 · Cost, performance and reliability

An AI workload’s cost is tokens times price for hosted models, and GPU-hours divided by useful tokens for self-hosted ones. Its performance is time to first token, time per output token and end-to-end latency at a given concurrency. Its reliability is mostly about capacity, throttling and agent behaviour rather than crashes. The levers have an order: route by difficulty, shrink the context, cache, batch, reserve capacity for the base load, and only then negotiate price.

From the job descriptionOptimize the performance, cost (token and inference economics), scalability, and reliability of AI workloads in partnership with Security, Cloud Platform, and SRE teams.
token economics
cost per call = input × p_in + cached × p_cached + output × p_out; cost per outcome = cost ÷ successes
inference economics
self-hosted $ per 1M tokens = GPU $/h ÷ (tokens/s × 3,600) × 10⁶, divided by utilisation
capacity
reserved throughput below the base load; pay-as-you-go spillover through gateway pools
SLOs
availability, time to first token and p95, quality, and cost per outcome, on one dashboard

The architecture moves the bill more than the price list does

The levers, in order

LeverMechanismOn AzureWatch for
1 · route by difficultyA small or fine-tuned model first, the frontier model for the hard tailAliases per difficulty; Foundry Model Router behind the default aliasTail quality: gate on it, calibrate the confidence
2 · shrink the contextBudgets per block, compact tool results, summarised historyThe context assembler (card 9)Dropping evidence the answer needed
3 · cacheIdentical prefixes; repeated questionsAutomatic prefix caching on supported models; API Management semantic cacheStale or cross-tenant answers: partition by consumer, keep the threshold low
4 · batchOffline work at about half priceGlobal Batch deploymentsTurnaround inside the batch window
5 · reserve the base loadProvisioned throughput for steady trafficPTU reservations; standard deployments as spillover in a poolPaying for idle: reserve below the base, review quarterly
6 · fine-tune or distilShorter prompts, a smaller model at volumeThe model factory (cards 3 and 4)A model to maintain
7 · negotiateCommitments and discountsWith Procurement and Cloud PlatformLock-in: keep the alias layer

Inference economics for self-hosted models illustrative

$ per 1M tokens = GPU $/hour ÷ (tokens/s × 3,600) × 10⁶ ÷ utilisation · $4/h, 2,500 tokens/s: $0.44 at full use, $1.48 at 30%

Utilisation, not the GPU price, decides self-hosted economics. Continuous batching (vLLM, Triton), quantisation to FP8 or INT4, prefix caching, speculative decoding and autoscaling on queue depth raise it; a model that sits idle overnight on a reserved GPU never beats an API.

Latency and reliability

latency ≈ queue + prefill(input tokens) + output tokens × time per output token

  • Fewer input tokens cut prefill and time to first token.
  • Fewer output tokens (structured outputs, short reasoning) cut decode time.
  • Streaming improves what users feel; parallel tool calls and a small model for intermediate agent steps cut the total.
  • Reserved throughput gives predictable latency; shared capacity gives cheaper variable latency.
FailureControl
429 throttlingSpillover pools, Retry-After honoured, backoff with jitter
Provider or region incidentMulti-region pools; a fallback alias
Agent loopsRuntime budgets; a loop-detection query
Tool outageCircuit breakers; answer without the tool and say so
Silent model changePinned versions; golden set on every remap
Cost spikeQuotas per consumer; burn-rate alerts

Working with Security, Cloud Platform and SRE

TeamOwnsThe CoE brings
SecurityIdentity, network, threat protection, penetration testsTool permission models, agent identities, the AI threat model (card 11)
Cloud PlatformLanding zones, quotas, reservations, infrastructure modulesCapacity forecasts per alias, the reservation case, AI-specific modules
SRESLO practice, incident process, on-callAI SLOs (quality and cost beside latency), runbooks for AI failure modes, the platform team on the pager for its own services

You have cut all three kinds of cost: cloud, GPUs and tokens

  • Noctal. Multimodal models “on GCP Vertex AI, GKE and GPU/TPU serving — 80% throughput uplift”. resume
  • Virtual Minds. A ranking model serving 10K QPS with daily updates: latency and capacity engineering under load. resume
  • The headline you sent. “Cost/token economics on Azure, AWS and GCP”; “scalability, resiliency, latency and cost optimization”; Kubernetes, Argo CD, CI/CD. resume

The line to useCloud cost at E.ON (25%), GPU throughput at Noctal (80%), token cost per step at Capital Group. The three economics the job description names (token, inference, infrastructure) are each a number you can quote.
Say it before they doBuying and sizing Azure provisioned throughput, and API Management’s token policies at enterprise scale, are study. GPU capacity planning and reservations on other clouds are production.

Cost, performance and reliability on Azure

  1. Meter. llm-emit-token-metric with consumer, tier, alias and workload dimensions; Cost Management exports joined to it for showback per team and per tenant.
  2. Limit. llm-token-limit per subscription (tokens per minute and a monthly quota); Cost Management budgets with action groups per workload; tighter quotas outside production.
  3. Route. Aliases per difficulty; cascades with calibrated confidence; Model Router behind the default alias for the easy majority.
  4. Cache. Stable prefixes by construction; the gateway’s semantic cache partitioned by consumer and alias, threshold near 0.05, enabled per product.
  5. Batch catalogue-scale and back-office runs through Global Batch.
  6. Capacity. PTU reservations for the base load in the primary region; standard deployments as spillover in the same backend pool, with a circuit breaker that trips on 429s and honours Retry-After; reviewed every quarter with Cloud Platform.
  7. Resilience. A second region in each pool; timeouts per alias; retries with jitter; circuit breakers on tools; a throttling drill each quarter.
  8. SLOs with SRE. Per-workload SLOs for availability, p95 and quality, burn-rate alerts, runbooks; the platform team carries the pager for the gateway, runtime and evaluation services.

Worked example: the chart, line by line illustrative

OptionArithmetic per million productsMonthly costAccuracy
frontier, real time1M × (900 × $2.50 + 60 × $10) ÷ 10⁶$2,8500.94
frontier, batchhalf of the above$1,4250.94
cascade, real time$100 for the small model on all + 15% × $2,850$5280.96
cascade, batch tail$100 + 15% × $1,425$3140.96

Batching the tail is possible because escalated products wait for an analyst’s approval anyway; the confident 85% return in real time. Cost per correct categorization falls from $3.03 to $0.33 per 1,000.

How AI cost and reliability go wrong

BadPrice per million tokens as the KPI.
GoodCost per outcome, after the quality gate.
BadReserving capacity for the peak.
GoodReserving below the base load and spilling the peak to pay-as-you-go.
BadRetrying a 429 immediately, in a tight loop.
GoodHonouring Retry-After, backing off with jitter, spilling to the next backend in the pool.
BadA semantic cache shared across tenants with a loose threshold.
GoodPartitioned by consumer and alias, a low threshold, enabled per product.
BadReporting median latency.
Goodp95 and p99 end to end, and time to first token for anything a person watches.
BadSelf-hosting a model without a utilisation plan.
GoodCost per million tokens at realistic utilisation, compared with the API, before the GPUs are bought.
BadTurning on full prompt logging and discovering the Log Analytics bill.
GoodContent recording by tier, sampling, and the platform’s own costs published beside the teams’.

Pools with spillover, quotas, metering and cache at the gateway; the cost query

// Bicep: reserved capacity first, pay-as-you-go spillover when the circuit breaker trips on 429s
resource chatEastPtu 'Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/backends@2024-06-01-preview' = {
  parent: apim
  name: 'chat-default-eastus2-ptu'
  properties: {
    url: 'https://${foundryEast}.openai.azure.com/openai'
    protocol: 'http'
    circuitBreaker: { rules: [ {
      name: 'trip-on-throttle'
      failureCondition: { count: 3, interval: 'PT1M', statusCodeRanges: [ { min: 429, max: 429 } ] }
      tripDuration: 'PT1M'
      acceptRetryAfter: true
    } ] }
  }
}
resource chatDefaultPool 'Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/backends@2024-06-01-preview' = {
  parent: apim
  name: 'chat-default-pool'
  properties: { type: 'Pool', pool: { services: [
    { id: chatEastPtu.id,   priority: 1, weight: 100 }     // reserved base load
    { id: chatSwedenStd.id, priority: 2, weight: 100 }     // spillover
  ] } }
}
<!-- inbound: quota, metering and a partitioned semantic cache -->
<llm-token-limit counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" tokens-per-minute="{{tier-tpm}}"
                 token-quota="{{tier-monthly-tokens}}" token-quota-period="Monthly" estimate-prompt-tokens="true" />
<llm-semantic-cache-lookup score-threshold="0.05" embeddings-backend-id="embed-v2-pool" embeddings-backend-auth="system-assigned">
  <vary-by>@(context.Subscription.Id)</vary-by>
  <vary-by>@((string)context.Variables["alias"])</vary-by>
</llm-semantic-cache-lookup>
<llm-emit-token-metric namespace="ai-platform">
  <dimension name="Consumer" value="@(context.Subscription.Name)" />
  <dimension name="Alias" value="@((string)context.Variables["alias"])" />
</llm-emit-token-metric>
<!-- outbound: <llm-semantic-cache-store duration="300" /> -->
// tokens and estimated cost by consumer and alias, last 30 days (prices kept in a platform table)
customMetrics
| where timestamp > ago(30d) and name in ("Prompt Tokens", "Completion Tokens")
| extend consumer = tostring(customDimensions["Consumer"]), alias = tostring(customDimensions["Alias"])
| summarize tokens = sum(valueSum) by consumer, alias, name
| evaluate pivot(name, sum(tokens))
| join kind=leftouter (PriceTable) on alias
| extend est_cost_usd = (['Prompt Tokens'] * input_price + ['Completion Tokens'] * output_price) / 1e6
| order by est_cost_usd desc
# the chart's arithmetic, and the self-hosted formula
def per_item(tok_in, tok_out, p_in, p_out):                    # $ per item, prices per 1M tokens
    return (tok_in * p_in + tok_out * p_out) / 1e6

frontier = per_item(900, 60, 2.50, 10.00)                         # $0.00285
small, tail = 0.0001, 0.15
for name, cost in {"frontier": frontier, "frontier batch": frontier / 2,
                   "cascade": small + tail * frontier, "cascade batch tail": small + tail * frontier / 2}.items():
    print(f"{name:<20} ${cost * 1e6:,.0f} per 1M items")          # 2,850 · 1,425 · 528 · 314

def self_hosted_per_million(gpu_per_hour, tokens_per_s, utilisation):
    return gpu_per_hour / (tokens_per_s * 3600) * 1e6 / utilisation   # 4, 2500, 0.3 -> $1.48

In the room

How do you control AI spend?Attribution first: token metrics by team, tier, alias and workload at the gateway, joined to the bill, so every team sees its cost per outcome. Then the levers in order: route by difficulty, shrink context, cache, batch, reserve capacity below the base load with spillover, and fine-tune or distil where volume justifies it. Hard quotas per consumer and budgets per agent run make every loop cost a bounded amount. On a categorization workload, a cascade with the tail batched cuts the bill by about nine times and is more accurate than the frontier model alone.
When does self-hosting a model pay?When utilisation is high and steady. Cost per million tokens is the GPU’s hourly price divided by tokens per hour, divided by utilisation: the same GPU is three times more expensive per token at 30% utilisation than at 90%. Continuous batching, quantisation and autoscaling raise utilisation; a fine-tuned small model on a busy volume task is the usual case where it beats an API.
What breaks first on an AI platform, and how do you keep it up?Capacity and behaviour, not crashes: throttling, agent loops, tool outages, silent model changes, cost spikes. Pools with reserved capacity first and spillover second, Retry-After honoured, a second region, budgets in the runtime, circuit breakers on tools, pinned model versions behind aliases, and burn-rate alerts on cost and quality as well as latency. I agree the SLOs with SRE and my team carries the pager for the platform services.
How do you work with Security, Cloud Platform and SRE?By owning the AI-specific part and nothing else. Security owns identity and the network; I bring the threat model for agents and tools. Cloud Platform owns landing zones and reservations; I bring the capacity forecast per alias and the case for a reservation. SRE owns the SLO practice; I bring quality and cost SLOs beside latency and the runbooks for AI failure modes.

13 · Leading cross-team work and reviewing designs

Leading an ambiguous initiative across value streams is mostly turning ambiguity into a small number of decisions with owners and dates, then getting teams that do not report to you to make them the same way. Design review is how standards reach the code of teams you do not manage. It works when it is tiered by risk, fast, run against criteria everyone can read, and more helpful than the alternative of shipping alone.

From the job descriptionLead the most complex, ambiguous, cross-team initiatives spanning multiple value streams, and review and influence AI designs across product teams to ensure alignment with enterprise standards.
frame first
the problem, the constraints, the metric that says done, and what is explicitly out of scope
decisions
reversible ones delegated with a deadline; one-way doors written up with options and dissent
design review
tiered by risk, criteria published, an answer within two working days, outcomes recorded
influence
the road is faster than the alternative; wins published with numbers; a consumer council that sees its requests land

A design review funnel: most designs never need a meeting

Running an ambiguous initiative across value streams

  1. Frame it on one page. The problem in the customer’s terms, the constraints, the metric that says done, the non-goals, and a decision log.
  2. Map the teams and their incentives. Who gains, who pays, who decides, who can block. Ambiguity is usually a disagreement nobody has named.
  3. Find the one-way doors early and decide them deliberately; delegate the reversible decisions with deadlines.
  4. Ship one slice end to end with one team (the lighthouse) before asking anyone else to change.
  5. Make the new path the default: a template, a migration done by the platform, a published comparison.
  6. Report on decisions, not tasks: which decisions are open, who owns them, when they close.
  7. Close it: measure the metric, retire the old path, write down what the next initiative should copy.

The published design-review criteria for an AI system

AreaThe questionCard
RiskWhich tier, and does the design carry that tier’s controls?11
DataIs every training or retrieval source registered with a rights basis; how is PII handled?5
ModelsWhich aliases, chosen on which evaluation evidence; what is the fallback?2
RetrievalAre entitlements enforced before ranking; are effective dates modelled?8
ToolsIs the tool surface within budget; do writes need approval; are servers behind the gateway?7
EvaluationIs there a golden set with blocking thresholds and an online quality SLO?10
CostWhat is the cost per outcome at expected volume, and which quotas cap it?12
OperationsWhat fails first, how is it detected, and how is it rolled back?12

How escalations arrive, and how they leave

Arrive withA one-page decision request: the question, the options, the criteria, the recommendation, what has been tried, and who disagrees.
Leave withA decision record inside a week, the reasoning, the dissent noted, a date to revisit, and everyone committed to the outcome.

  • Capital Group. “Delivery plans balancing quality, cost and risk”, with editorial and legal reviewers as stakeholders. resume
  • Allianz. Models built “with actuaries and digital stakeholders”. resume
The line to useEvery one of your last three roles was leadership without line authority over the people who had to change: client teams at TEKHQS, business units at E.ON, research and DevOps at Noctal. That is exactly the shape of a Senior Principal in a Center of Excellence.
Say it before they doA formal enterprise architecture board at a large product company is new. You have run architecture reviews for an organisation and influenced a utility’s business units; present the tiered funnel as how you would scale that.

How you would run it at Vertex

  1. First 30 days: listen and map. Meet each product team building AI across the value streams; list their workloads, models, data, tools and pain; find the overlaps (three teams building the same retrieval, two building the same evaluation harness).
  2. Publish the review process: criteria, templates for the design doc and the decision record, the reviewer rotation, the two-day answer target, and where outcomes are recorded.
  3. Start a consumer council with one engineer per product team; its requests become the platform roadmap, and it sees them land.
  4. Pick the first cross-team initiative from the overlaps, where one shared service saves several teams work, and lead it yourself.
  5. Grow the reviewer bench: Staff and Principal engineers rotate through reviews with you before they review alone (card 14).

Worked example: one tax-content retrieval service for three products illustrative

StepWhat happens
The ambiguityA copilot, a categorization explainer and a configuration agent each index tax content their own way; answers disagree, refresh cycles differ, nobody owns effective dates
The frameOne retrieve serving all three; stale-rule answers below 1%; p95 under 800 ms; non-goal: changing any product’s UI
One-way doorsWho owns the index (the CoE); the effective-date model; the entitlement model
LighthouseThe copilot moves first; its golden set becomes the shared regression suite
Default pathThe platform migrates the other two, runs both indexes in parallel for two weeks, and compares on their golden sets
CloseThree indexes retired; one owner; the stale-rule rate tracked as an SLO

How cross-team leadership fails

BadArriving with the solution.
GoodArriving with the problem, the metric and a question; the solution is shaped with the teams.
BadStatus reports about tasks.
GoodStatus reports about decisions: open, owner, date.
BadDesign review as a gate teams try to avoid.
GoodDesign review as fast, published help; the escape-hatch rate is the measure of whether it is.
BadEvery review in a meeting.
GoodAsynchronous first, meetings for the few that need them, every outcome written down.
BadWaiting for consensus on everything.
GoodDecide, record the dissent, commit, revisit on a date.
BadHeroics: the principal who fixes every team’s design personally.
GoodSystems: criteria, templates, linters, a reviewer rotation.

The templates that make review cheap

# design.md front matter, checked by a linter in the pull request that adds the design
---
workload: tax-content-qa
tier: medium                       # low | medium | high (card 11)
owner: team-copilot
aliases: [chat-default, embed-v2]  # must exist in the inventory and be allowed at this tier
data_sources:
  - {name: tax-content, rights: owned, pii: none}
  - {name: product-docs, rights: owned, pii: none}
retrieval: {service: retrieve, filters: [tenant, groups, jurisdiction, effective_date]}
tools: []                           # MCP servers behind the gateway only
evaluation: {golden_set: golden/tax-qa-v12.jsonl, gates: {groundedness: 4.2, citation_precision: 0.95}}
cost: {expected_calls_per_month: 400000, cost_per_outcome_usd: 0.012, quota_tokens_month: 1.2e9}
rollback: alias remap to chat-default@previous
review: async                       # async | architecture | authority (set by the linter from tier and scope)
---

In the room

Tell me about leading an ambiguous, cross-team initiative.At E.ON I started with one analytics use case and grew it into four production AI systems and a fifteen-person function, without authority over the business units that used them. What worked was framing each problem in the business’s terms with a metric, delivering one slice they could see, and then making our way of building the default for the next use case. I translated executive use cases into architectures, roadmaps and acceptance criteria, so the decisions were explicit and owned.
How do you review designs across many teams without becoming the bottleneck?A funnel. Published criteria and a template that a linter checks settle most designs. A rotating Staff or Principal reviewer answers asynchronously within two days for the next band. Architecture review is for high-tier or cross-cutting designs, and I close only the one-way doors and the disagreements the criteria cannot settle, in a written record. If teams start routing around review, that is my bug to fix.
How do you influence teams you do not manage?I make the right way the fastest way, publish results with numbers, give teams a council whose requests visibly land, and do the migration work for them when we change something. As a consultant at TEKHQS every engagement starts without authority: at Capital Group the editorial and legal reviewers had to choose to trust what we built before any of it could ship.
Tell me about a hard trade-off.At Capital Group I kept the compliance knowledge graph advisory: it tells the agent which rules and disclosures apply, but it never enforces them, because a model policing itself is not a control. Enforcement is deterministic checks plus human legal review, and the hard-enforcement path, if ever needed, is a policy-check step that blocks. The cost was more work in the review step; the benefit is a control an auditor can trust.
Tell me about a failure.Use a real one, in this shape: what happened and its impact, the root cause stated plainly, what you changed that day, and the guardrail you added so it cannot recur (a budget cap, a validation step, a gate, a human checkpoint). Ownership without blame, and what the organisation learned, not only you.

14 · Multiplying the organization

A Senior Principal’s output is measured in other engineers’ decisions. Growing Staff and Principal engineers means widening their scope from a system to an area to the organisation, teaching them to write the documents that move people, and giving them real decisions with a safety net. Raising the AI engineering bar means making good practice the default (evaluation before shipping, data rights before training, budgets before agents) so that it holds when you are not in the room.

How to frame itYou have grown data scientists and engineers into leads, and run hiring and architecture reviews. Growing Principals is different in one way: they already have the skills, so what you give them is scope, decisions and visibility. Say that distinction; it shows you know the job.
Say it before they doPromoting engineers to Principal is not on your resume. Do not claim it; describe how you would do it, with the mechanisms on this card, and point to the teams you built at E.ON and Noctal.

The first ninety days with the Staff and Principal engineers

  1. One-to-ones with each of them: what they want to own, what is blocking them, which decision they would most like to make.

  4. Write the AI engineering bar as one short page, then encode every line of it in a template or a CI check; the page links to where each is enforced.
  5. Open office hours and a guild; the platform roadmap takes contributions from product teams.
  6. Agree a growth plan with each person and review it monthly: scope now, scope next, the decision they own this quarter, the document they will write, what you will sponsor.

In the room

How do you grow Staff and Principal engineers?By growing their scope, not their skills; at that level the skills are there. Each of them owns a real decision with me as the safety net, writes the document that moves other teams, reviews designs in a rotation where I review their reviews, and leads an initiative where I am the escalation and not the lead. Then I sponsor the work, with their name on it, in the rooms where promotions are decided.
How would you raise the AI engineering bar here?Write it on one page and then make every line of it a default: evaluation evidence enforced by a CI gate, data rights by the training pipeline, budgets and approvals by the agent runtime, the tool standard by a linter, cost per outcome by the design template. Talks and guilds help people understand the bar; templates and gates are what keep it when nobody is watching.
Tell me about someone you grew.Use a real person from the E.ON Smart Agents team or Noctal, in this shape: where they started, the decision or scope you handed them, how you supported without taking over, what they delivered, and where they are now. At E.ON you built and led a fifteen-person team, so pick the story with the clearest change of scope.
How do you know you are multiplying, not just busy?Fewer decisions reach me, more designs pass review first time, people I sponsor get promoted or given scope by others, and the standards show up in teams’ code without my asking. If my calendar is full of reviews only I can do, I am the bottleneck, and the fix is training reviewers.

How to run a scenario: the 45-minute flow, the Vertex lens, the AI-first frame

A scenario interview scores how you think, not what you know: whether you clarify before you design, whether the architecture has a reason for every box, where you put a model and where you refuse to, what you measure, and what you give up. The role exists to help Vertex become an AI-first organization, which means two motions at once: AI embedded in the products customers already run (the tax engine, Copilot, Smart Categorization) and new AI applications built beside them (the Configuration Agent, e-invoicing intake). Every scenario on cards A to E is one of those two motions, and every answer ends with what it leaves behind for the next team: a paved road, a golden set, a standard.

From the job descriptionFull-spectrum lifecycle … traditional AI/ML, GenAI and software architecture … reference architectures and paved roads … leading cross-team initiatives … long-term direction while hands-on.
two motions
embed AI in an existing product · build a new AI application beside it
the flow
clarify → frame → architecture → agentic → engineering → evaluation → trade-offs → close
the lens
the engine decides · evidence on every output · effective dates · data rights · approval until earned
what they score
structure · trade-offs said out loud · numbers · judgement about autonomy · what you leave behind

Forty-five minutes, eight moves, and the board filled left to right

  1. Clarify (5). Three questions, chosen from the bank on the Clarifying questions tab. Say why each one changes the design: “if the reviewers are the constraint, the architecture optimises the queue, not the tokens.”
  2. Frame (2). Say the Vertex lens in one breath and name the motion: embed or new. Write both at the top of the board. Everything after refers back to them.
  3. Architecture logic (10). Boxes with reasons. Start from the data and the engine, add the model where the input is language-shaped or the path is open, and draw the evidence trail from every output back to its source. Name what is bought, wrapped and built.
  4. Agentic logic (8). Which step is agentic and why; the tools it sees (fewer than ten); what is read-only; the deterministic validation it cannot override; the approval; how autonomy is earned per change class.
  5. Engineering logic (8). Numbers in a corner: volume, peak, latency budget, cost per unit, capacity. Then the mechanics: queues, batch, idempotency, retries with jitter, quotas at the gateway, durable state.
  6. Evaluation and safety (5). The golden set and who labels it; the metric that matches the business (revenue-weighted accuracy, field-level F1, straight-through rate); the online signal; the grounding check; the data rights.
  7. Trade-offs (3). What you would cut if the deadline halved; what you would add with twice the budget; the one risk you cannot design away and how you would tell the customer.
  8. Close (1). What the next team reuses: the cascade pattern, the change-set contract, the numeric grounding check, the capacity-per-alias rule.

The whiteboard template

Top line

The lens in five words and the motion (embed or new). The interviewer sees the frame before the boxes.

Middle

The engine and the system of record in the centre; the AI layer beside it, never above it; data sources on the left; the people (reviewers, approvers, customers) on the right.

Corner

The numbers: volume, peak, latency, cost per unit, human capacity. Labelled “for example” and used to make one decision each.

Bottom

The evaluation loop as an arrow back into the design: golden set, online signal, what changes when the signal moves.

Five rules that make an answer sound like it was built for a tax company

  • The engine decides; AI proposes, explains and automates around it. The tax determination is deterministic and auditable; a model never computes tax. It categorises, extracts, proposes configuration, narrates a calculation, drafts a resolution. In every scenario, point at the box where the engine sits and say “this one does not change.”
  • Every output carries evidence and an audit trail. Category plus confidence plus the passages or examples it rested on plus the model version plus who approved it. In tax, the audit package is the product as much as the answer is.
  • Effective dates and jurisdictions everywhere. A rate, a rule, a registration, a mapping: all valid from a date, in a place. Retrieval filters on both; the golden set is dated; a change feed, not memory, answers “what changed.”
  • Customer data stays the customer’s. Catalogues, invoices and transactions train customer-scoped adapters unless the contract says otherwise; EU data stays in an EU data zone; retention follows statute; PII is minimised before a model sees it.
  • A human approves anything that changes a tax outcome until evidence earns autonomy, per change class. Shadow, then assist, then self-serve, one class at a time, with the agreement and incident rates as the gate. Autonomy is a measured property, never a setting.
