AI-first means two motions and one road under both

An AI-first organization is not one where every team has a chatbot. It is one where every product team can add a model to a product in weeks because the road is paved, and where new AI applications are built on the same road instead of beside it. The Senior Principal’s job is to make both motions repeatable: the reference architecture, the paved roads, the standards, the design review and the people who can run them without you.

Embed AI in an existing productBuild a new AI application
where the value isa step customers already do, done faster or with less review: categorising, explaining a calculation, resolving an exceptiona job nobody could do at this scale before: configuring an ERP from a change event, reading a million PDFs a day
what stays fixedthe product’s contract: the engine, the data model, the audit trail, the customer’s workflowthe platform contracts: the gateway, aliases, retrieve, the agent runtime, the approval primitive
the riskbreaking trust in a product customers already rely on; a wrong answer looks like the product being wrongbuilding a one-off that routes around the road; autonomy granted before it is earned
the first metricthe step’s own metric moves: review time, straight-through rate, revenue-weighted accuracyagreement with humans in shadow mode, then incident rate as autonomy grows
what it leaves behinda pattern other product teams copy: the cascade, the grounding check, the exception loopa contract other agents reuse: the change set, the capability id, the sandbox gym
scenariosA (Smart Categorization at scale), C (Copilot answers), D (keeping the embedded AI reliable)B (the configuration agent), E (e-invoicing intake on the acquisition)

The road under both motions, on the cards

One gateway, aliases, retrieve

Cards 1, 6 and 8. Every model call and tool call accounted for; a model swap without a code change; retrieval with tenant, entitlement and effective-date filters.

Golden sets as gates

Card 10. No change ships without its golden set; judges calibrated against people; online evaluation on sampled traces.

Capacity and cost as products

Card 12. Quotas, priority pools, cost per unit on a dashboard, burn-rate alerts. The embedded AI stays reliable at quarter-end.

People who can run it

Cards 13 and 14. Published review criteria, decision records, Principal and Staff engineers who own a motion each.

Say it this way“AI-first is a property of the organization, not of a product. The test is whether the fifth product team can embed a model as fast as the first did, and whether the next new application is built on the same road. That is what the reference architecture and the paved roads are for, and it is why I would spend my first ninety days on the road rather than on one application.”

The question bank: pick three, and say why each one matters

  • Who is the user, and what decision do they make with the output? A tax analyst who approves wants evidence; an AP clerk who posts wants a yes or no; a customer who reads wants a citation. The user decides the output shape and the autonomy level.
  • What is the volume, the peak, and the deadline? Volume decides batch or interactive; the peak decides capacity; the deadline decides what you cut. Ask for all three; interviewers often give one.
  • What does “wrong” cost, and in which direction? Under-collection is a liability for the customer; over-collection is refunds and complaints; a wrong registration is both. The cost of wrong sets the precision threshold and the approval step.
  • What exists today? The engine, the content and its effective dating, prior mappings, labelled data, the gateway. Reusing the engine’s output as validation is the strongest move in most scenarios.
  • What can we change, and what can we only read? Read-only ERP access shapes the whole agent design; a sandbox tenant makes test quotes possible; no sandbox means shadow mode first.
  • Which region, which residency, which retention? EU data zone or not; statutory retention; whether customer data may train anything. Ask early; it changes which services you can use.
  • How is success measured by the business? Reviewer hours saved, straight-through rate, time to configure, escalation rate. Design to that metric, and say which proxy you would measure first.
BadTen questions in a row, then a design that uses none of the answers.
GoodThree questions, each followed by “so the design will …”, and the answers written on the board where the design can point at them.
BadAsking for the budget before asking what wrong costs.
GoodCost of wrong first; it sets the threshold, the approval and the budget you will need.

What a scenario rubric usually scores, and what strong looks like

DimensionWeakStrong

evaluation“we would test it”a golden set with named labellers, a business-shaped metric, a calibrated judge, an online signal, and what changes when it moves

Time traps

  • The deep dive at minute 8. If they probe a detail early, answer in two sentences and say “I will come back to that in engineering logic”; then do.
  • Defending the first design. When they change a constraint, change the design out loud: “with no sandbox, validation moves to shadow mode; the approval step stays.”
  • The number you do not have. Say “for example”, pick a round one, and show the arithmetic. They score the arithmetic, not the number.
  • Skipping evaluation to finish the drawing. An unfinished drawing with an evaluation loop beats a finished one without.

Openers and closers for any scenario

The opener“Before I draw anything, three questions, because each changes the design: who makes the decision with the output, what does a wrong answer cost and in which direction, and what can we read versus change in the systems involved.”
The frame“I will design this the way everything in a tax business should be designed: the engine decides, AI proposes and explains around it, every output carries its evidence, dates and jurisdictions are everywhere, and a person approves anything that changes a tax outcome until the evidence says it can run alone. This one is an embed-into-the-product scenario, so the product’s contract stays fixed.”
When they change a constraint“Good, that moves one thing: …” and then move exactly one thing on the board.
When they ask for the number you don’t have“For example, call it a million a day; then the arithmetic is … and the decision it drives is …”
The close“If the deadline halved I would cut the frontier tier and widen the human queue; the thing I cannot design away is label quality, so I would tell the customer the interval, not the point. What the next team gets from this is the cascade pattern and the audit package contract, which is the point of doing it on the road rather than beside it.”

A · “A retailer sends 2.1M SKUs and goes live in ten days. Categorize them.”

Smart Categorization at scale: an embed-into-the-product scenario. Vertex describes Smart Categorization as its first commercial AI product, GPT-based models with tax intelligence and machine learning, with a confidence score, an approval step and audit packages Vertex data sheet, Apr 2026. The scenario tests the training-strategy, fine-tuning and cost lines of the job description, and whether you notice that the real constraint is reviewer hours, not tokens.

The prompt, as they might put it“A large retailer signed last week. They have 2.1 million SKUs with descriptions and some attributes, and they go live on the first of the month, ten days from now. Every SKU needs a product class so the engine can tax it. We have eight analysts. How do you do it?”
motion
embed: the product’s contract (classes, confidence, approval, audit package) stays fixed
volume and deadline
2.1M SKUs · ten days · eight analysts
the constraint
reviewer throughput, not model cost
what they test
JD lines: training strategy · fine-tuning · cost and reliability · evaluation

Clarify first: three questions that each change the design

  • Which taxonomy, and which jurisdictions do they sell into? The product classes are fixed; the jurisdictions decide where a wrong class costs money. Rate variance across the jurisdictions sold into is what ranks the human queue.
  • What comes with each SKU? Description only, or attributes, UNSPSC codes, images, prior mappings from their old system? Prior mappings become the mapping memory and remove a third of the work before any model runs.
  • What accuracy did the customer sign up to, and how many reviews can an analyst do in an hour? The accuracy sets the auto-accept threshold; the review rate sets the size of the queue you can afford.

The frame in one sentence

“Ten days is a throughput problem with an accuracy constraint: dedupe to families, run a cascade that sends only the hard cases to people, rank that queue by revenue at risk, and ship an audit package per SKU.”

What a strong answer shows

Classic ML and LLMs together

A fine-tuned classifier with calibrated confidence does most of the work; the frontier model with retrieval takes the long tail. That is the training-strategy line of the job description in one design.

The engine stays the engine

The output is a product class plus evidence. The engine taxes; the model never decides a rate.

The human queue as a designed object

Risk-ranked, batched by look-alikes, with the rationale pre-filled. Reviewer hours are the budget you manage.

The number you commit to

Revenue-weighted accuracy with an interval, told to the customer early, with what happens if the golden set disappoints.

A pipeline, not a chat: dedupe, then a four-tier cascade, then an audit package

Why each box is there

BoxWhat it doesWhy it is thereBought, wrapped or built
normalise, dedupestrip size, colour and pack variants; group into product familiescuts 2.1M to ≈ 600k decisions; variants share a classbuilt (rules + embeddings)
mapping memoryexact and near matches to approved mappings: this customer’s history, the taxonomy historymost consistent tier; zero model cost; improves every daybuilt on AI Search (hybrid)
fine-tuned classifiera small model trained on approved mappings, with calibrated confidencecheap, fast, consistent; precision known per confidence bandbuilt (card 4)
frontier + retrievalthe frontier alias with the class definitions and nearest approved examples in contexthandles the long tail the classifier has never seenbought via the gateway alias
human queueanalysts review with the rationale pre-filledthe only tier that can be wrong on purpose and fix the othersbuilt (the product’s approval step)

Very little agency, on purpose

The steps are known, so code orders them. One agentic piece earns its place: an evidence gatherer for the families the classifier and the frontier model both left uncertain.

Evidence gatherer

For a low-confidence family, pulls the spec sheet, the attributes, the manufacturer page if licensed, and the nearest approved examples; drafts the rationale for the reviewer in three lines with citations.

Tools it sees

get_family(id), search_approved(text, k), get_class_definition(code), fetch_spec(url). Four tools, all read-only. Nothing writes a mapping.

Guards

Step and cost budget per family; retrieved text labelled untrusted; the draft goes to the queue, never to the engine.

Why not more

An agent that chooses the class itself is the frontier tier wearing a costume. The value is in the evidence, and evidence is what the reviewer scores.

Bad“An agent categorises each SKU, calls the engine to check, and retries until it is confident.”
GoodA cascade with known tiers; an agent only where the path is open: gathering evidence for the hard 8%.
BadThe model writes the class to the engine when confident.
GoodOnly the approval step writes; auto-accept is an approval policy with a precision threshold, recorded like a human approval.

The numbers that make the decisions illustrative

600k × (1 − 0.35) = 390k → × (1 − 0.70) = 117k → × (1 − 0.60) = 47k to people · 8 × 6 × 120 = 5,760 reviews per day · 47,000 ÷ 5,760 ≈ 8.2 days
frontier: 900 in + 60 out tokens per family at $2.50 / $10 per M = $2.85 per 1,000 · 117 × 2.85 ≈ $333 · Global Batch halves it

Tokens cost hundreds of dollars; reviewer hours are the budget. So the engineering goes into the queue:

  1. Rank by revenue at risk. Score each family by revenue × the spread of rates it could land on across the jurisdictions sold into. A $5M family that could be exempt or taxable goes first; a $50 family with one possible rate goes last.
  2. Batch look-alikes. Group the queue by nearest-neighbour clusters so a reviewer decides a pattern once and applies it to twenty families.
  3. Pre-fill the rationale. The evidence gatherer’s three lines and the two nearest approved examples sit beside each item; the reviewer confirms or corrects, rarely researches.
  4. Run the model tiers on day one. Memory and the classifier finish in hours; the frontier tier goes through Global Batch overnight; the queue is full by day two and the analysts are never waiting on a model.
  5. Feed approvals back. Every approved class enters the mapping memory the same hour, so families that arrive later in the load resolve without a model.
  6. Plan the fallback. If the queue runs long, raise the classifier’s auto-accept coverage only where the calibration curve allows it, and tell the customer which families will go live as “provisional, under review” with the audit package saying so.

Measured the way the business feels it: revenue-weighted, with an interval

  • Golden set. 2,000 SKUs sampled across the customer’s categories, weighted toward high-revenue families, labelled by tax research before the model tiers run. Report revenue-weighted accuracy beside plain accuracy: a wrong $5M SKU is not a wrong $50 SKU.
  • Calibration, not a single threshold. Precision per confidence band on the golden set; auto-accept only in bands at or above 0.98. A model is allowed to be unsure; it is not allowed to be confidently wrong without a person.
  • Swapping models. McNemar on the same golden set when the classifier is retrained or the frontier alias moves; 31 vs 111 discordant pairs gives χ² ≈ 44, which is a real difference, and a tie is a reason to keep the cheaper one.
  • Online signal. The correction rate in the human queue per tier and per category, weekly. A category whose correction rate rises is a category the classifier has drifted on; retrain or route it to the frontier tier.
  • The interval, told early. If the golden set shows 460 of 500 right, say 89–94%, not 92%. The customer can plan for an interval; a point estimate that misses costs trust.
Data rights and safetyThe customer’s catalogue trains a customer-scoped adapter and nothing shared unless the contract says otherwise; approved mappings enter the shared taxonomy history only as class-level statistics. Descriptions can contain personal data in odd places (a seller’s name in a title); the normaliser redacts before anything reaches a model. Every audit package is retrievable by SKU for as long as the customer’s retention policy says.

What they will push on

  • “The golden set comes back at 0.91.” Keep the bar, reduce auto-accept coverage: more families go to people. Then more analysts or more days, and the customer gets the numbers on day two, not day nine. The design does not change; its dials do.
  • “Why not just run the frontier model on everything?” It would cost a few thousand dollars, which is fine. But a classifier fine-tuned on this customer’s approved mappings is better calibrated and more consistent on their vocabulary, the audit trail is cleaner, and the human queue ends up the same size either way. The frontier tier is for the tail.
  • “Where does the fine-tuned classifier come from on day one?” From the taxonomy history and prior customers’ approved mappings as a base, then a customer-scoped adapter trained on the first day’s approvals. If there is no base, the frontier tier takes the classifier’s place for this load and the classifier is trained for the next one.
  • “What if the descriptions are terrible?” Then the evidence gatherer matters more: attributes, UNSPSC codes, images if available (a vision-capable alias for the tail only), and the customer’s own old mappings. And the interval widens, and you say so.
  • “How do you keep the analysts from rubber-stamping?” Seed the queue with known-answer items (about 2%) and track agreement per analyst; show the rationale after the decision for a sampled share, not before.
  • “What would you cut with five days instead of ten?” The frontier tier: send its 117k straight to a wider queue ranked harder, add analysts, and go live with the bottom of the ranking provisional. Never the golden set.

In the room

The one-minute answer“Ten days is a throughput problem with an accuracy constraint. I dedupe 2.1 million SKUs into about 600 thousand product families, then run a cascade: mapping memory first, a fine-tuned classifier that auto-accepts only where its precision is proven, a frontier model with retrieval for the tail through batch, and a human queue for the hard eight percent, ranked by revenue at risk. Every SKU ships with an audit package. Tokens cost a few hundred dollars; reviewer hours are the budget I actually manage, so the engineering goes into the queue.”
The engine line“The output is a product class with evidence. The engine taxes it; nothing here decides a rate.”
The trade-off line“If the set comes back at 0.91 I keep the bar and widen the queue; I tell the customer the interval on day two. If the deadline halves I cut the frontier tier, not the golden set.”
What the next team gets“The cascade and the audit-package contract are the reusable parts: the same pattern categorises exemption certificates and invoice lines.”

B · “Design the agent that configures the tax setup when a customer’s ERP changes.”

A new-application scenario, in the setting of Vertex’s Configuration Agent for Microsoft Dynamics 365, which the announcement describes as detecting changes such as new entities, registrations or locations and applying the tax configuration they need Vertex announcement, 25 Nov 2025. This is the agentic-logic scenario: it tests the orchestration, MCP and tool-surface lines of the job description, and whether you know where an agent stops and code starts.

The prompt, as they might put it“A customer adds a legal entity, a new warehouse in Texas, or registers in a new state. Today a consultant updates the tax configuration by hand over two weeks. Design an agent that does it. How much of it runs on its own?”
motion
new application on the platform contracts: gateway, MCP, agent runtime, approval
volume
≈ 6,000 runs a month across customers; minutes are fine; days of approval wait are normal
cost of wrong
a wrong registration or mapping is a tax liability; both directions hurt
what they test
JD lines: orchestration and abstraction · MCP and tool surface · safety · evaluation

Clarify first

  • Which change events, and how do we see them? New legal entity, new ship-from location, new product line, a nexus threshold crossed, a registration in a new state. An ERP event feed makes the trigger code; no feed means a nightly diff, which changes the latency story.
  • Who approves today, and how long does it take them? If a tax consultant approves in two weeks, an agent that proposes in ten minutes with evidence is the product; the approval step is not the bottleneck, the research is.
  • Is there a sandbox tenant we can run quotes against? Test quotes through the engine before and after a change are the strongest validation available. No sandbox means shadow mode first.

The frame in one sentence

“It is a workflow with agents inside it, not an agent with a workflow inside it: the model proposes and explains, code validates with test quotes, a person approves, and apply takes an id, never a prompt.”

What a strong answer shows

Durable workflow outside

Eight known steps ordered by code, checkpointed, resumable after a two-day approval wait. The open parts (which rules, what change set) are the agentic steps.

A small tool surface

Three MCP servers, fewer than ten tools visible at any step, read-only wherever possible, and one write tool that only takes a validated, approved id.

Validation the model cannot override

Schema, referential integrity and test quotes are code. The model’s proposal is an input to validation, never its judge.

Autonomy earned per class

Shadow, assist, self-serve, per change class, with agreement and incident rates as the gate. “How much runs on its own” is answered with a measurement, not an opinion.

Eight steps; three are agentic; one writes, and only with an id

The change set is the contract

FieldExampleWho fills itChecked by
change_set_idcs_8f2…config server on proposeapply refuses any id not in state validated + approved
triggernew ship-from location, Austin TX, effective 1 Novdetect (code)idempotency key per event

A supervisor, three specialists, three MCP servers, one capability

Supervisor

Owns the run inside the workflow’s agentic steps: asks Facts, then Rules, then composes the proposal. Budgets enforced by the runtime: 12 steps, $0.50, five minutes per step.

Facts specialist

Reads the ERP: entity, locations, products, existing registrations. Tools: erp_entity_get, erp_locations_list, erp_products_sample. Read-only server, on-behalf-of identity.

Rules specialist

Retrieves registration and product-class rules as of the effective date, with citations. Returns “no evidence” when nothing clears the score floor; it never guesses.

Validator

Not a model. Schema, referential integrity, then config_validate re-quotes a sample of transactions through the engine and diffs. A failed validation goes back to propose once, then to a person.

The tool surface at each step

StepTools visibleWrites?Guard

applyconfig_apply(change_set_id) (called by code)yesonly ids in state validated + approved; scoped write identity; idempotent
BadOne agent with forty tools, including config_apply(entries), decides when it is done.
GoodFewer than ten tools per step; apply takes an id the model never minted; code decides when the run is done.
BadERP text (vendor names, item notes) flows into the prompt as instructions.
GoodERP fields arrive as typed, labelled data; the supervisor’s instructions say what to do with data, and the runtime strips anything that reads like an instruction.

Cost is irrelevant, so spend it on being right illustrative

  1. Durable execution. Every step checkpoints to Cosmos DB; a run waits days at approve and resumes on the same trace. Container restarts and model outages lose nothing.
  2. Idempotency twice. An idempotency key per ERP event stops duplicate runs; apply is idempotent on the change-set id so a retry never double-applies.
  3. Validation that costs something. Re-quoting 200 recent transactions through the engine is the expensive part of a run and the most valuable; budget the engine calls, not the tokens.
  4. Strongest model, exhaustive validation. Latency in minutes is fine, so the frontier alias with reasoning on propose, and a second independent proposal when the quote diff is large, compared before a person sees either.
  5. Rollback is a change set too. Every applied change set carries its inverse; verify failures apply the inverse and open a new run with the failure as evidence.
  6. One trace end to end. Gateway, runtime, MCP servers and engine calls share the operation id; the trace is the audit record the customer can ask for.

A gym before production; autonomy earned per change class

  • The sandbox gym. A library of seeded ERP states (sandbox tenants) with the expected change set for each: 50 at launch, grown from every production run a person corrected. Graded on exact match of the structured change set plus the quote diff. Runs in CI on every prompt, tool or model change.
  • Rollout per change class. Shadow: the agent proposes, people configure as before, agreement is measured. Assist: people approve the agent’s proposal. Self-serve: low-risk classes (a product-class mapping for an existing registration) run alone once agreement is above the bar for a quarter and the incident rate is zero. A new registration never leaves assist without a tax lead’s sign-off.
  • Online signals. Agreement rate per class, edit distance between proposal and approved version, time to approval, verify failures, rollbacks. A class whose edit distance rises goes back a stage.
  • Red-team with the ERP. Injected instructions in item descriptions and vendor notes; a sandbox state that contradicts the rules content; an approval that arrives for a stale proposal. All in the gym, all scheduled.
Safety and identityThe agent acts on behalf of the user who triggered the run and never holds standing write rights; apply runs under a scoped identity that can write configuration and nothing else. ERP content is data, never instructions. The approval shows the diff, the citations and the quote diff, so the approver is approving evidence, not a summary.

What they will push on

  • “Why not let it apply directly? The customer wants hands-off.” Because a wrong registration is a tax liability, the approval step costs minutes, and autonomy is earned per class with evidence. Hands-off is the destination; shadow and assist are how you get there without an incident on the way.
  • “What if the content doesn’t cover the rule?” The Rules specialist returns “no evidence”, the run goes to a person with the question stated, and the question becomes a content ticket. It never guesses.
  • “Single agent or multi-agent?” Specialists only where the context differs: ERP facts and tax content are different worlds with different tools. Otherwise one model with a small surface. Co-located in one runtime; split over A2A only if another product needs the Rules specialist on its own.
  • “Which framework?” The contracts matter more than the framework: gateway, MCP registry, approval primitive, OpenTelemetry. Microsoft Agent Framework on Foundry Agent Service is the paved road; the same design runs on LangGraph on Container Apps.
  • “How do you test an agent?” The gym: seeded states, expected change sets, exact-match grading plus the quote diff, in CI. Plus the online agreement rate, which is the only test that counts once it is live.
  • “What breaks first in production?” Stale proposals: the ERP changes again while the approval waits. Verify catches it, and the fix is a freshness check on the facts before apply, which is a cheap re-run of the Facts step.

In the room

The one-minute answer“A durable workflow with eight steps: detect, facts, rules, propose, validate, approve, apply, verify. Three steps are agentic, because the questions are open: which facts matter, which rules apply, what the change set should be. Validation is code: schema, integrity, and re-quoting recent transactions through the engine. A person approves the diff with its evidence. Apply takes a change-set id that has passed validation and approval; the model never mints one and a prompt can never reach apply. Autonomy is earned per change class: shadow, assist, self-serve, with the agreement rate as the gate.”
The tool-surface line“Three MCP servers behind the gateway, fewer than ten tools visible at any step, read-only wherever possible, one write tool with one argument.”
How much runs on its own“Today, the research and the proposal. In a quarter, the low-risk classes end to end, because the gym and the agreement rate will say so. A new registration stays with a person until the numbers argue otherwise.”
What the next team gets“The change-set contract and the capability-id pattern. Every agent that changes anything in a Vertex product gets the same shape: propose, validate in code, approve, apply by id.”

C · “Customers ask Copilot why an invoice was taxed at 8.25% and what the rate for SaaS in Texas is from July. Make the answers trustworthy.”

An embed scenario on Vertex Copilot: the product already exists, the question is how to extend it to tax questions without putting a number in a customer’s hands that the model made up. It tests the retrieval line of the job description end to end (chunking, hybrid search, re-ranking, effective dates), the evaluation line (golden sets, calibrated judges, grounding), and the lens rule that the engine, not the model, is the source of a number.

The prompt, as they might put it“Copilot answers product questions today. Customers want it to explain their own calculations and answer rate and rule questions. Legal is nervous. Design it so a tax analyst would trust it, and tell me how you would know it is trustworthy.”
motion
embed: Copilot’s contract stays; the new intents sit behind a router
volume and latency
≈ 50k turns a day · first token under 2.5 s · p95 under 8 s
cost of wrong
a wrong number in writing, with the Vertex name on it
what they test
JD lines: RAG end to end · evaluation and observability · safety and responsible AI

Clarify first

  • Who asks: a tax analyst or an AP clerk? The analyst wants the rule and the citation; the clerk wants “yes, this is right”. Same system, two answer shapes; the router carries the persona.
  • Can we reach the transaction’s calculation record? If the engine’s calculation log is available by transaction id, the explanation question has a deterministic source and the model only narrates. If not, the explanation intent is out of scope until it is.
  • How is tax content versioned and effective-dated, and is an answer ever “advice”? Effective dating decides the retrieval filters; the advice question decides the wording policy and the refusals.

The frame in one sentence

“Trust comes from where the numbers come from: numbers come from the engine or the content, never from the model; the model narrates and cites with effective dates; anything it cannot ground, it says so.”

What a strong answer shows

Intents with different sources

Explaining a calculation and answering a rule question are different problems with different truth sources. A router that knows the difference is the architecture.

Retrieval built for tax

Hybrid search, semantic re-ranking, and filters for jurisdiction, effective date and tenant. A rate without a date is wrong by default.

A grounding check you can show Legal

Every number in the answer traced to a tool result or a passage, or the answer does not ship. A mechanism, not a promise.

Evidence of trust

A golden set written with tax research, a judge calibrated against analysts, an interval instead of a point, online correction rates per jurisdiction.

One router, four lanes, one grounding check before anything streams

Retrieval built for tax content

StageDesignWhy
chunkingby document structure: one rule, one rate row, one definition per chunk, with jurisdiction, effective-from and effective-to in metadataa rate row without its dates is the most common wrong answer
queryhybrid (keyword + vector) on AI Search; filters on jurisdiction, as_of and tenant before ranking; semantic ranker on the top 50statute numbers and codes need keyword; paraphrases need vector; filters before ranking keep recall honest
assemblya token budget per section: record first, passages second, history last; duplicates removed by chunk idthe truth source is never the part that gets trimmed
answerstructured: claim, number, citation id, effective date; rendered after the grounding checkstructure is what makes the check mechanical
updatesblue/green index swap when monthly content lands; a retrieval regression suite gates the swapcontent changes monthly; the swap is a release

Minimal and tool-bound: three read tools, no writes, two ways to stop

Tools

get_calculation(transaction_id) returns the engine’s record; search_rules(query, jurisdiction, as_of) returns passages with ids and dates; changes_since(date, jurisdiction) returns the feed. All read-only, all tenant-scoped by the caller’s token.

Clarify

When jurisdiction or date is missing and the answer depends on it, the model asks one question instead of assuming. “Texas, and from which date?” is a correct answer.

Abstain

When nothing retrieved clears the score floor, or the grounding check fails twice, the answer is “I can’t ground that; here is who can” with the support route. Logged as an abstention, which is a metric.

Why not an agent loop

The path is not open: each intent has a known source and a known shape. A loop would add latency and ways to be wrong without adding an answer the lanes cannot give.

BadOne prompt with the whole tax guide in context and “answer carefully”.
GoodIntent-specific lanes with their own truth source, a structured answer, and a check that reads the structure.
BadThe model computes the tax to explain it.
GoodThe engine’s record is fetched; the model explains the record; a mismatch between content and record is reported, never resolved by the model.

Latency budget, cost per turn, and the index as a release illustrative

turns per day
50k
interactive; weekday peaks at month-end
first token
< 2.5 s
router + retrieval + first stream chunk
p95 full answer
< 8 s
including the grounding check
cost per turn
≈ $0.019
small router + frontier answer + re-rank
monthly
≈ $28k
50k × 30 × $0.019
budget: router 150 ms · retrieval 300 ms (hybrid + semantic ranker) · prompt cache hit on the fixed prefix · first token ≈ 1.2 s · grounding check runs on the structured draft before render
  1. Two models. The small alias routes and clarifies; the frontier alias answers. The router’s cost is noise; its latency is what you tune.
  2. Prompt caching. The lane instructions, the answer schema and the citation rules are a fixed prefix; only the record, the passages and the question vary.
  3. Stream after the check. The structured draft is checked for grounding before rendering, then the rendered answer streams. It costs a few hundred milliseconds and removes the worst failure.
  4. The index is a release. Monthly content lands in a new index; a retrieval regression suite (known questions, expected chunk ids) runs; the alias swaps blue/green; the old index stays for a rollback window.
  5. Quotas at the gateway. Copilot has its own consumer quota and the interactive priority class (scenario D). It never competes with a batch job.
  6. Traces. One operation id across router, retrieval, model and check; the trace carries the chunk ids and the record id, which is how an analyst audits an answer later.

How you would know it is trustworthy

  • The numeric grounding check. Every number, rate, date and jurisdiction in the structured draft must appear in a tool result or a retrieved passage; otherwise regenerate once, then abstain. Mechanical, logged, and the first thing to show Legal.
  • The golden set. 500 questions written with tax research across intents and jurisdictions, with the expected number, citation and effective date. 460 right is 89.3–94.1% on a Wilson interval; report the interval, and report it per lane, because the explanation lane should be near 100% and the rule lane carries the risk.
  • A calibrated judge. An LLM judge grades correctness, citation support and wording policy; it is calibrated against analyst grades on 200 items (agreement, then disagreement review) before it grades alone, and re-calibrated when the model or the content changes.
  • Online. Escalation rate, “corrected by a human” rate, abstention rate, per jurisdiction and per lane, weekly. A jurisdiction whose correction rate rises is a content problem until proven otherwise.
  • Retrieval on its own. Recall@10 on the regression suite gates every index swap; retrieval failures are the cause behind most answer failures and are cheaper to find there.
Safety and wordingExplain, don’t advise: the wording policy forbids recommendations and includes the effective date in every cited rate. The out-of-scope lane refuses legal questions and anything about other vendors’ systems, and the refusals are evaluated like any other intent. Customer transaction data stays in the tenant: the calculation record is fetched with the caller’s token and never enters a shared index or a training set.

What they will push on

  • “The content and the engine disagree.” The engine’s calculation is what was charged; the answer says so, cites both, and flags the discrepancy to the content team through the trace. The model never papers over a disagreement.
  • “How do you stop it answering legal questions?” A router class with explicit refusals and its own golden set. Refusals are evaluated; a refusal rate that drops is a regression.
  • “Why not fine-tune on the tax content?” Content changes monthly and retrieval with effective dates updates in a day; a fine-tune does not. Fine-tune the tone and the answer format if anything, never the facts.
  • “What about long documents, tables, rate matrices?” Chunk by structure, not by size: a rate row with its header and dates is one chunk; a matrix becomes rows. Hybrid search finds codes; the ranker orders paraphrases.
  • “How do you handle a question about a date in the future?” as_of takes it; if no content is effective then, the answer says the current rule and that nothing later is published, with the date it checked.
  • “What would you cut with half the time?” The change-summary lane; the explanation and rule lanes with the grounding check are the product. Never the golden set, never the check.

In the room

The one-minute answer“Trust comes from where the numbers come from. A router sends each question to a lane with its own truth source: the engine’s calculation record for explanations, effective-dated retrieval over the content for rule questions, the change feed for what changed, and a refusal for legal advice. The model narrates and cites; it never produces a number. Every number in the draft is traced to a record or a passage before the answer streams, or we abstain. I would know it is trustworthy from a 500-question golden set written with tax research, reported as an interval per lane, a judge calibrated against analysts, and the correction rate per jurisdiction online.”
The Legal line“The grounding check is a mechanism, not a promise: here is the log line that shows the number, the passage and the date it came from.”
The retrieval line“Chunk by structure with dates in the metadata, filter before ranking, hybrid then semantic re-rank, and treat the monthly index swap as a release with its own regression suite.”
What the next team gets“The numeric grounding check and the structured answer schema; they drop into any product that puts a number in front of a customer.”

D · “It’s quarter-end. Copilot p95 went from 3 s to 14 s, 9% of calls return 429, and AI spend doubled in two weeks. Go.”

The cost, performance and reliability scenario, and the one where they watch how you think under pressure. It is about keeping embedded AI reliable once several products share the same models: the job description’s line about performance, cost and reliability with Security, Cloud Platform and SRE. The strong answer has three horizons (the next hour, the next week, the next quarter) and ends with gates, not heroics.

The prompt, as they might put it“It is the last week of the quarter. Copilot is slow, customers are seeing errors, finance is asking why the Azure OpenAI bill doubled, and SRE has paged you. What do you do in the next hour, the next week, and the next quarter?”
motion
platform: the road under every embedded model
symptoms
p95 3 s → 14 s · 429s at 9% · spend 2× in two weeks
first move
protect the interactive path; then find the cause; then make it structural
what they test
JD lines: performance, cost and reliability · working with SRE · standards that stick

Clarify fast: the questions are the first diagnostic step

  • What changed in the last two weeks? Deploys, new consumers on the gateway, prompt changes, a new batch job. Spend doubling in two weeks is a change, not a trend.
  • Which alias is saturated, and who are the top consumers by tokens? The gateway’s token metric per consumer answers both in one query. If there is no such metric, that is finding number one.
  • Is there a provisioned pool, and who is on it? If interactive traffic shares pay-as-you-go capacity with a batch job, the fix for the next hour is already visible.

The frame in one sentence

“First I protect the interactive path, then I find the cause, then I make it structural: capacity per alias, priority pools, admission control, and a CI gate on tokens.”

What a strong answer shows

Order of operations

Stop the bleeding before diagnosing; diagnose before fixing; fix with a gate, not a patch. Say the three horizons out loud and keep them separate.

The gateway as the lever

Quotas, priority, metrics, and the retry policy all live in one place. If every call goes through the gateway, the first hour is configuration; if not, the first week is making it so.

Arithmetic

Tokens × calls × price, with the retry multiplier. A root cause you can show as a number is one finance believes.

Working with SRE

SRE owns the pager, the dashboards and the postmortem format; you own the AI-specific levers and the gates. Say who does what.

Capacity per alias, three priority pools, and why 70% is the number

Capacity as a product: what each alias declares

AliasPriority classCapacityQuota per consumerSLO
chat-defaultinteractiveprovisioned, target ρ ≤ 0.7, spillover to pay-as-you-gotokens per minute by productp95 < 4 s · 429 < 0.5%
